Day 1 · Spotlight paper

MolmoAct2

An open robot foundation-model recipe spanning pretraining, mid-training and adaptation. The talk connects visual understanding and physical reasoning to an action expert, and discusses out-of-the-box deployment plus external evaluation.

Research details
How it worksJoin a vision-language backbone with an action expert, then train through pretraining, mid-training and task adaptation.
Why it mattersAn open recipe makes model, data and evaluation choices inspectable by researchers rather than hiding them behind a demonstration.
Open questionWhich parts of out-of-the-box success survive a genuinely new robot, task and environment?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

Semantic Anchoring for Robotic Action Representations

Examines how action representations can drift away from the semantics of pretrained vision-language models during narrow robot fine-tuning. It proposes separating shared semantic alignment from private physical-execution features.

Research details
How it worksSeparate semantic features aligned to a frozen vision-language reference from private features needed for physical execution.
Why it mattersNarrow robot fine-tuning can lose useful language semantics even when training-task success improves.
Open questionDoes alignment retain instruction following without removing task-specific geometric detail?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

MEM

Adds memory at two temporal scales to VLA policies: compressed recent video and recurrent, textual long-term state. The speaker shows how these help with multistep tasks and adapting after past mistakes without keeping all raw frames in context.

Research details
How it worksCompress recent video into short-term context and retain recurrent textual state over longer task horizons.
Why it mattersRemembering what has already happened can prevent repeated cleaning or losing track of multistep goals.
Open questionCan the memory recover from an incorrect stored belief, and how is old state cleared between tasks?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

PRTS

Recasts pretraining as learning a representation of progress toward an instruction-specified goal rather than only predicting demonstrated actions. Contrastive reachability objectives are combined with action prediction before downstream behavior-cloning adaptation.

Research details
How it worksCombine action prediction with instruction-conditioned contrastive goal-reachability pretraining.
Why it mattersA representation of progress can distinguish useful intermediate states from merely imitating the next demonstrated movement.
Open questionDoes reachability supervision transfer to new goals without requiring their trajectories in the pretraining set?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

Learning What to Say to Your VLA

Instead of updating a frozen VLA, learn which language instructions elicit better behavior. The system searches for useful local language sequences, trains a feedback policy from interaction, and gates language interventions when they are likely to help.

Research details
How it worksSearch for language sequences that steer a frozen VLA and learn a feedback policy that intervenes selectively.
Why it mattersChanging the instruction can improve execution while preserving the base policy's pretrained capabilities.
Open questionHow often does language steering help, and when is missing low-level skill the actual bottleneck?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

When Vision Overrides Language

Investigates counterfactual VLA failures where familiar visual scenes override the instruction. A benchmark and inference-time guidance compare language-conditioned with unconditioned action predictions to strengthen language following.

Research details
How it worksEvaluate counterfactual instructions in familiar scenes, then contrast conditional and unconditional action predictions at inference.
Why it mattersA robot can appear competent while following visual habits rather than the requested task.
Open questionDoes improved instruction following persist across unseen scenes and ambiguous language?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

ZETA

A controlled study of cross-embodiment transfer that separates strict zero-shot evaluation from cases where the target robot appeared in pretraining. Results emphasize gripper-local action coordinates, adequate source-robot coverage, and clear disclosure of target exposure.

Research details
How it worksHold scenes and tasks fixed while varying robot embodiment and action-coordinate representations.
Why it mattersStrict zero-shot transfer and target-exposed pretraining answer different questions and need separate reporting.
Open questionHow much transfer comes from gripper-relative coordinates, source diversity or prior exposure to the target robot?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

EmbodiSteer

Keeps a Cartesian action policy frozen but performs denoising and constraint guidance in the target robot's joint space. This allows a shared policy to account for each robot's collision geometry without abandoning task-space behavior.

Research details
How it worksGuide denoising in the target robot's joint space while keeping the learned Cartesian policy frozen.
Why it mattersThe gripper can follow the intended path while the rest of an unfamiliar arm collides; embodiment-aware execution addresses that gap.
Open questionHow reliable is collision avoidance under geometry errors or unfamiliar joint limits?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

Diagnosing Compositional Generalization

Asks which task combinations must actually appear in training to support new multi-step compositions. The experiments separate coverage gaps, instruction steering failures, and dependencies between subgoals.

Research details
How it worksDecompose compositional failures into instruction shift, coverage of combinations and dependencies between subgoals.
Why it mattersA sparse dataset may suffice for independent subtasks yet fail when one stage changes the conditions required by the next.
Open questionWhich dependent task pairs must be demonstrated, and which combinations can be composed without new data?

Day 1 · Keynote

Hang Zhao — Organizing Physical AI Across Timescales

Organizes physical intelligence around the different clocks at which a robot must operate. The keynote compares coded policies, direct model control, orchestration and agentic skill use under a real wall-clock budget, then separates slower task reasoning from motor execution and fast contact response. A high benchmark success rate can hide an impractical inference delay.

Research details
How it worksCompare coded policies, direct reasoning, orchestration and agentic skill use under a wall-clock budget, then separate task reasoning, skill execution and fast control.
Why it mattersA model's success rate does not establish a useful robot if the robot spends most of its time waiting for inference.
Open questionWhat latency and feedback frequency does each physical subtask require, and where should computation be placed?

Day 1 · Oral paper

RoboTTT

Scales robot-policy context using test-time training and fast-weight state rather than retaining an ever-growing raw history window. The presentation studies how task-relevant experience can influence behavior across long sequences. This is online internal-state adaptation; it should be distinguished from an autonomous research agent retraining a policy through experiments.

Research details
How it worksUse test-time training and fast-weight state to retain task-relevant experience across long robot sequences.
Why it mattersLong-horizon context need not be stored as an ever-growing raw observation window.
Open questionHow do online state updates behave after a failure, interruption or change of task?

Mem-World

Uses a memory-augmented, action-conditioned world model for robot manipulation. The system queries stored multi-view spatial history based on prospective actions, rather than treating all historical visual evidence as equally important.

Research details
How it worksCondition a world model on actions while retrieving relevant multiview spatial history from memory.
Why it mattersAction-dependent retrieval can preserve hidden object and scene information that current images omit.
Open questionHow does the model handle stale or contradictory history, and does better video prediction improve control?

Day 1 · Industry / sponsor

Sharpa

Sharpa presents a dexterous-manipulation stack built around three complementary paths: more useful demonstrations, turning reference behaviors into executable skills, and reusing interaction experience across embodiments. Its central argument is that hand-motion video alone leaves out contact, force and recovery information required for reliable manipulation. This is a sponsor presentation, not a controlled comparison of all approaches.

Research details
How it worksCombine demonstration capture, reference-to-skill conversion and cross-embodiment experience in a dexterous manipulation stack.
Why it mattersUseful dexterous data must describe contacts, forces and recovery as well as visible hand motion.
Open questionWhich parts of the stack have controlled independent validation, and what acquisition cost is needed per reusable skill?

Day 1 · Industry / sponsor

Lightwheel

Lightwheel describes a data-to-simulation-to-deployment workflow: capture human activity, build or calibrate simulated environments, train and evaluate robot policies, then use deployment feedback to improve the loop. The talk emphasizes measuring whether simulated interactions reproduce real physical behavior, rather than assuming visual similarity guarantees useful transfer. Product and performance claims are presented by the company.

Research details
How it worksCapture real activities, calibrate simulation, train and evaluate policies, then return deployment feedback to the simulator.
Why it mattersA useful simulation loop must reproduce interaction outcomes, not only realistic-looking imagery.
Open questionHow is physical fidelity checked against real trajectories, and does simulator improvement reduce deployment failures?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

BitVLA

BitVLA explores ultra-low-bit vision-language-action models for edge deployment. Its training recipe combines low-bit language/vision alignment, quantization-aware distillation, and robot-policy training, with a specialized runtime for packed weights. The engineering question is how much memory, energy and latency can be saved without losing manipulation performance; the comparisons are speaker-reported.

Research details
How it worksTrain native low-bit vision-language-action components using alignment, quantization-aware distillation and a runtime for packed weights.
Why it mattersMemory, power and inference delay determine whether a model can run onboard a physical robot.
Open questionDo performance and energy gains hold on the intended edge hardware under matched precision and control budgets?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

EagleVLA

EagleVLA targets onboard real-time control where cloud latency or limited edge compute can make action predictions stale. It combines future-state anticipation with asynchronous inference and scheduling so a robot can react to more recent observations while maintaining coherent motion. The talk evaluates control frequency, observation-action alignment and real-world task execution, not just raw model throughput.

Research details
How it worksAnticipate the future state during inference and schedule perception, action prediction and execution asynchronously.
Why it mattersFaster throughput alone does not fix actions that are already stale when the robot executes them.
Open questionHow much prediction error can the controller tolerate when the world changes during its inference delay?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

REACT

REACT addresses a latency-versus-smoothness trade-off in action-chunking policies. Longer chunks produce coherent motion but can become outdated when objects move; shorter chunks react faster but may be jittery. Rolling denoising revises an ongoing action sequence using fresh observations, allowing the controller to respond without discarding all temporal consistency. It is a reactive-control method, not agentic self-improvement.

Research details
How it worksUse rolling denoising to revise a long action sequence with fresh observations while preserving temporal continuity.
Why it mattersResponsive reactive control and smooth motion can coexist without repeatedly discarding the whole action chunk.
Open questionHow do input freshness, reaction delay and motion jitter trade off on dynamic physical tasks?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

TARC

TARC turns the control-update rate into a learned decision. Instead of replanning at a fixed frequency, a policy selects both an action and how long to hold it, subject to an explicit update budget. The talk applies this idea to locomotion and VLA-style control, asking when expensive inference is actually necessary to retain successful feedback control.

Research details
How it worksLearn an action together with its holding duration under an explicit budget on control updates.
Why it mattersInference can be concentrated at disturbances rather than spent at a fixed rate even when the robot is stable.
Open questionWhat minimum update rate preserves recovery when unexpected contact or a push occurs?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

Diffusion ReRoll

Diffusion ReRoll changes how denoising progresses across time in robot sequence prediction. Conventional full-horizon and causal schedules can commit early to a poor motion prefix; partial re-noising keeps earlier and later steps open to revision. The speaker reports stronger sequence behavior on challenging trajectories and argues that the noise schedule itself is a useful temporal inductive bias.

Research details
How it worksPartially re-noise sequence regions so earlier and later timesteps can continue revising one another.
Why it mattersA poor early motion prefix need not become irreversible simply because its denoising finished first.
Open questionHow much extra inference is required, and does the benefit persist with the same training schedule and model capacity?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

MoRE

MoRE proposes a mixture-of-motion-experts design for 3D world models spanning different material and actuator dynamics. A router selects among specialized motion experts rather than forcing a single dynamics model to average incompatible regimes. The recorded presentation was interrupted early by technical problems, so this entry describes the stated approach but does not claim verified empirical results.

Research details
How it worksRoute interactions to specialized motion experts within a shared 3D world model covering different physical regimes.
Why it mattersAveraging incompatible material dynamics can hide the motion needed for reliable prediction.
Open questionThe recorded talk ends early after technical problems; empirical performance requires the paper or a complete presentation.

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

Targeting World Models to Compromise Robot Learning Pipelines

This paper studies a security failure mode of robot-learning pipelines that use third-party demonstrations and generative world models. An attacker perturbs seemingly ordinary visual inputs so the world model generates undesirable behavior under an otherwise benign task prompt; training on those generations can contaminate the downstream policy. The result is a warning about data provenance and model-mediated amplification, not an endorsed attack technique.

Research details
How it worksInvestigate whether compromised third-party demonstrations can contaminate a robot policy through generated world-model data.
Why it mattersSynthetic data can amplify provenance problems in its input rather than making a learning pipeline trustworthy.
Open questionWhat screening, provenance tracking and downstream validation detect contaminated generated trajectories?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

Chunk-wise Model-based Policy Optimization

Chunk-wise Model-based Policy Optimization replaces repeated one-step imagined rollouts with a model that predicts a future latent chunk from the current state and a proposed action chunk. The goal is to obtain useful multi-step optimization signals while reducing recursive model error and backpropagation-through-time instability. The talk reports simulation and bipedal-control experiments; numerical comparisons remain speaker-reported.

Research details
How it worksPredict a future latent chunk from the current latent state and an action chunk, then optimize through that model.
Why it mattersChunk-level modeling can reduce recursive rollout error and unstable long-horizon gradients during training.
Open questionDoes the model remain accurate as chunk length grows, and what physical tasks expose model bias?

Day 1 · Spotlight paper

FedGuide

FedGuide considers federated reinforcement learning when robot clients have different dynamics, rewards or initial states. Instead of naively averaging policies, it uses diffusion-based prior alignment and a value-based baseline so each client can retain useful specialization while learning from shared information. The evaluation probes return and stability under heterogeneous settings.

Research details
How it worksAlign client-specific diffusion priors through a shared server while keeping locally specialized policies and stabilizing value estimates.
Why it mattersRobots with different dynamics and goals need knowledge sharing that preserves useful local behavior.
Open questionDoes sharing help the weakest client without collapsing distinct behavior modes or requiring incompatible objectives?

Day 1 · Keynote

Wolfram Burgard — Challenges to Realize Embodied AI

Argues that robust embodied autonomy requires more than broad learned perception and action: uncertainty, calibrated confidence, task-stage evaluation and failure handling still matter. The keynote relates older probabilistic-robotics ideas to current foundation models and practical deployment requirements. The useful question is whether confidence and recovery remain reliable after the robot leaves familiar conditions.

Research details
How it worksCombine learned perception and action with calibrated uncertainty, task-level evaluation and the requirements of deployed robotic systems.
Why it mattersProbabilistic reasoning and explicit failure handling remain valuable when broad models encounter real physical uncertainty.
Open questionAre confidence estimates calibrated at each task stage, including after the robot has already deviated from the intended plan?

Max Insights

Max Insights presents its infrastructure for collecting human and robot interaction data and connecting that data to robot-learning feedback loops. The talk discusses egocentric capture, translating human experience into robot-relevant training material, and monitoring whether deployed actions meet intended goals. These are company-described capabilities rather than peer-reviewed benchmark conclusions.

Research details
How it worksBuild egocentric capture and processing infrastructure, then connect task monitoring to data and improvement loops.
Why it mattersThe usefulness of a data pipeline depends on whether its output resolves actual robot-learning bottlenecks.
Open questionHow are label quality, embodiment transfer and downstream improvement measured independently of collection volume?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Ego2Robot

Converts egocentric human activity videos into robot-oriented demonstrations by aligning hand actions and visual appearance. The talk evaluates whether synthesized human-to-robot data improves generalization when mixed with robot data for pretraining.

Research details
How it worksRecover human motion, replay or retarget it in simulation, overlay a robot into the source scene and filter synthesized examples.
Why it mattersHuman footage becomes more useful when both action and visual mismatches are addressed.
Open questionWhich gains come from action alignment versus visual synthesis, and what failures survive filtering?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

BiDexGrasp

BiDexGrasp studies coordinated two-hand grasps for objects whose size and geometry make single-hand grasping impractical. It combines faster grasp-data synthesis with a learned model that explicitly couples the hands and uses object-relative anchors. The presentation reports simulation, cross-platform and physical-grasp evaluations, distinguishing coordination from simply generating two independent grasps.

Research details
How it worksGenerate coupled bimanual grasp data and train a model with explicit object-relative coordination between hands.
Why it mattersTwo independently plausible grasps may conflict when both hands must support one object together.
Open questionDo coordinated grasps remain feasible under real contact uncertainty and a different hand embodiment?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

KP-Grasp

KPGrasp represents dexterous grasps as 3D hand keypoints instead of directly predicting wrist poses and joint angles. A flow-matching transformer models the conditional keypoint distribution; inverse kinematics then recovers executable robot commands. The design aims to reduce bespoke grasp losses and test-time optimization while scaling across object shapes and partial point-cloud inputs.

Research details
How it worksModel grasp distributions in a 3D hand-keypoint space, then recover joint commands through inverse kinematics.
Why it mattersA common geometric representation can reduce bespoke joint-space loss design and support partial observations.
Open questionWhat fraction of predicted keypoint grasps remains kinematically and contact-feasible after inverse kinematics?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

WM-Craftnet

WM-Craftnet combines depth, tactile sensing, proprioception and interaction history in a recurrent world-model representation for dexterous in-hand manipulation. Predicting cleaned geometry and tactile state acts as a training signal even when deployed observations remain noisy. The talk argues that a world model can serve as a reusable state representation for closed-loop contact control, not only a generator of imagined futures.

Research details
How it worksFuse depth, touch, proprioception and history in a recurrent representation trained to predict cleaned geometry and tactile state.
Why it mattersWorld-model training can improve a state representation without requiring online imagined-rollout search.
Open questionDoes representation quality improve closed-loop control under new sensor corruption and contact conditions?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Sequential Asymmetric Imitation

Sequential Asymmetric Imitation learns coordinated two-robot behavior without requiring simultaneous teleoperation of both robots. First one robot is trained; then the second is demonstrated alongside that frozen policy, and the first is corrected for the interaction. This exposes each policy to the other robot's real timing and mistakes, improving waiting, yielding and shared-object handling relative to independently trained policies.

Research details
How it worksTrain one robot first, demonstrate a partner alongside its frozen policy, then correct the first robot for the resulting interaction.
Why it mattersStaged data collection exposes each policy to its partner's timing and mistakes without simultaneous dual teleoperation.
Open questionCan the learned pair still coordinate if one robot or its controller is replaced?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Leave It Better Than Found

Leave It Better Than Found studies sequential collaboration between independently trained robots sharing an environment. A leading robot may achieve its own task yet leave an obstacle that makes the follower's task impossible. The method uses the follower's value estimate, gated by out-of-distribution checks, to guide how the leader leaves the environment, without joint policy training.

Research details
How it worksUse a follower's value estimate, with an out-of-distribution gate, to guide how a leading robot leaves shared state.
Why it mattersFinishing one's own task is insufficient if it makes the next robot's task impossible.
Open questionDoes the value gate still protect cooperation when the follower encounters a genuinely new shared state?

RL Token

Day 2 · Oral paper

Neuro-symbolic motion prediction

This neuro-symbolic motion-prediction talk combines neural trajectory forecasts with probabilistic logic encoding context-dependent traffic rules. A learned trust gate decides when rule-based reshaping should influence the predicted trajectories, since road users do not always obey formal rules. The reported gains are concentrated in difficult or unusual cases, highlighting both the value and limits of explicit constraints.

Research details
How it worksCombine neural motion forecasts with probabilistic traffic rules and a learned gate for trusting symbolic guidance.
Why it mattersRules can help rare cases while allowing for road users who do not follow those rules.
Open questionHow does the gate behave under incorrect maps, local-rule changes and deliberate noncompliance?

Roberto Martín-Martín — Learning Without Starting Over

OpenDexGrasp

OpenDexGrasp considers grasps that are suitable for a requested downstream task, not merely physically stable. For example, holding a container securely is insufficient if the grasp blocks the part a robot needs to use. The approach connects open-vocabulary language goals with object contact and grasp generation, asking whether grasp selection can anticipate intended manipulation affordances.

Day 2 · Oral paper

FACTR 2

FACTR 2 estimates external joint torque on inexpensive robot arms using signals already available from the motors and a model learned from free-space motion. The estimated force signal is then used to train force-aware manipulation policies without adding a dedicated force-torque sensor. This reframes contact sensing as a calibration and representation problem as well as a hardware problem.

Research details
How it worksLearn the arm's free-space motor-current response, estimate external joint torque as a residual, and use that signal in force-aware policies.
Why it mattersCommodity arms may gain useful contact feedback without a dedicated force-torque sensor.
Open questionHow robust is the estimate to payload, temperature, wear and motion outside the calibration distribution?

Day 2 · Oral paper

PACE

PACE separates tactile information into distinct temporal roles for precision insertion. Sustained touch indicates the current contact phase, abrupt changes trigger corrections, and prediction of future tactile evolution supplies an auxiliary learning signal. This structure is intended to handle ambiguous visual states during insertion more effectively than treating tactile input as just another concatenated feature.

Research details
How it worksUse persistent tactile state for action conditioning, abrupt tactile events for correction and future touch prediction for training.
Why it mattersTouch serves different temporal roles during alignment, insertion and recovery.
Open questionDoes the phase/event split generalize across sensors, objects and contact speeds?

Day 2 · Oral paper

Disco / distilled search

DISCO learns long-horizon rearrangement through progressive-widening tree search in GPU-parallel physics simulation. A learned policy proposes continuous actions, a value function guides search, and search outcomes repeatedly update both. The trained policy-value model is then deployed directly without simulator-based search at test time. The presentation reports improved rearrangement and sim-to-real results; those outcomes have not been independently reproduced here.

Research details
How it worksDuring training, use progressive-widening MCTS with learned continuous-action proposals and value guidance, periodically distill search outcomes into the policy and value model, and repeat. Deploy the resulting model directly without simulator-based search at test time.
Why it mattersMoves expensive future reasoning into training so a deployed policy can benefit from long-horizon search without paying its simulator-based runtime cost.
Open questionDoes the distilled policy retain long-horizon success on new arrangements without additional test-time search?

RoboNaldo trains humanoid soccer shooting through a staged reinforcement-learning curriculum built from a reference kicking motion. Day 2 · Spotlight paper

DeTac

DeTac addresses a sensing conflict in vision-based tactile sensors: embedded markers help estimate force but obscure surface texture. A dual-branch model separates marker/force information from appearance, with cross-branch supervision and paired measurements. The talk demonstrates why preserving both tactile geometry and texture matters for downstream perception.

Research details
How it worksSeparate tactile shading/texture from markers used for force estimation with a dual-branch model and cross-branch supervision.
Why it mattersThe same tactile image can contain useful surface detail and marker interference that should be disentangled.
Open questionDoes separation remain accurate for new materials, lighting and sensor deformation?

Finger Eye

FingerEye places complementary cameras inside a fingertip so a dexterous hand can sense both approach and near-contact interaction continuously. The method combines the visual streams with contact-relevant features for manipulation policies. The reported experiments compare wrist-only vision, one-camera sensing and contact-only tactile feedback on precision tasks.

Why it mattersNear-contact vision can bridge the gap between a distant wrist view and touch that only appears after contact.

DAVATaR

DAVATaR studies manipulation across the air-water interface, where refraction degrades vision and submerged electronics complicate tactile sensing. It combines depth-aware visual augmentation with pressure-transmitting fingertip sensing that keeps sensitive electronics above the water. The work treats underwater contact as a joint perception-and-hardware problem.

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Demystifying When and Why VLAs Fail in Contact-Rich Tasks

Diagnoses two contact-rich VLA bottlenecks: generating precise small actions and responding to temporally structured force information. The presentation changes the post-training noise schedule and introduces short-history, contact-gated force conditioning. These mechanisms target execution and feedback deficiencies rather than visual recognition alone.

Research details
How it worksImprove fine-action post-training with a different noise schedule and inject temporally structured, contact-gated force signals.
Why it mattersPrecision and contact feedback are separate failure modes that a strong visual backbone alone may not solve.

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Constraint-Decomposed Impedance Control

Constraint-Decomposed Impedance Control infers motion directions consistent with an articulated object's kinematic constraints from samples of a generative policy. It assigns higher stiffness along feasible directions and more compliance in directions likely to create unwanted forces. The approach uses the policy's own trajectory distribution to guide contact-safe execution without requiring a manually specified constraint model for every object.

Research details
How it worksEstimate an articulated object's feasible motion subspace from generative-policy samples and assign direction-dependent impedance.
Why it mattersPolicy uncertainty can guide compliance so stiff tracking does not convert small motion errors into large forces.
Open questionHow reliable is the inferred subspace when articulation changes with configuration or policy samples are biased?

TAM

TAM is a small torque-adaptation module that compensates for differences between nominal robot dynamics and actual payload, friction or hardware. It uses recent motion history to adjust torque commands, and can be trained in simulation using randomized free-space interactions. The talk tests this adapter across control policies without fully retraining each underlying policy for a new robot.

How it worksUse recent motion history in a fast torque adapter trained with randomized simulation dynamics.
Why it mattersPayload and friction differences can be corrected below the policy interface, allowing several controllers to reuse the same adapter.

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Combining Constrained Sampling and RL

This paper separates the exploration problem in manipulation reinforcement learning from the policy-optimization problem. It constructs a physically constrained state-sampling distribution using contact and feasibility knowledge, so the learner encounters useful modes of interaction more frequently. The hypothesis is that better structured starting conditions can outperform prolonged exploration from arbitrary states.

Research details
How it worksSample physically feasible contact states from explicit constraints, then use resets or curricula to guide reinforcement learning.
Why it mattersPrior physical knowledge can make useful interaction modes easier to discover without handcrafting every reward.

Physics-Guided Residual Dynamics

Physics-Guided Residual Dynamics combines an approximate physics simulator with a learned correction for deformable-object motion. Surface particles and velocities estimated from RGB-D observations are simulated using physics, then a residual network adjusts the prediction. Rope and brush-like objects illustrate why neither unconstrained learning nor a hand-tuned physics model is always sufficient on its own.

How it worksPredict a physics-based deformable-object step and learn the residual correction from interaction data.

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Cloth simulator-in-the-loop

This cloth-manipulation method uses a simulator as a forward model during inference. A learned reconstruction maps an observed cloth image to a deformable mesh; parallel simulated rollouts then refine a candidate action sequence, and the robot executes the first action before replanning. Unlike a purely reactive policy, it explicitly spends test-time computation to evaluate physical consequences.

Research details
How it worksReconstruct a cloth mesh from the current image, refine action candidates with parallel simulator rollouts and execute the first action before replanning.
Why it mattersExplicit inference-time physics can correct a policy's proposed action using anticipated physical consequences.
Open questionHow sensitive is planning to cloth reconstruction errors and imperfect simulator dynamics?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Robustness without Wrinkles

Robustness without Wrinkles develops differentiable deformable-object simulation and robust model-predictive control. Smooth approximations make optimization through contact dynamics tractable; parallel simulation and feedback control account for uncertainty during manipulation. It illustrates the alternative to end-to-end behavior cloning when one can afford physics-based planning at runtime.

Research details
How it worksDifferentiate through deformable-object simulation and use robust output-feedback model-predictive control with parallel computation.
Why it mattersA model-based controller can account for uncertainty rather than relying on one nominal predicted motion.
Open questionWhich uncertainty and smooth-contact assumptions are required for the claimed robustness or certification?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

NICE — Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding for 3D Manipulation Policies under Depth Corruption

NICE trains spatial features that remain useful when depth measurements are unreliable, especially for transparent or reflective objects. Cross-view geometry supervision and uncertainty-aware feature aggregation seek to avoid brittle reliance on corrupted depth pixels. Physical grasping examples examine whether the learned representation transfers to conditions where conventional 3D policies struggle.

Research details
How it worksTrain cross-view-consistent geometry features and uncertainty-aware spatial aggregation for corrupted depth observations.
Why it mattersDepth sensors can be unreliable on reflective or transparent objects even when RGB clearly shows them.
Open questionDoes robustness extend to unseen corruption patterns and camera calibration errors?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Spatial-temporal feature map mobile manipulation

Conditions mobile manipulation on an accumulated spatiotemporal environment and robot feature map. Explicit spatial history helps a policy handle tasks that extend beyond one tabletop view or one immediate action. The central deployment concern is whether that map remains accurate when the robot revisits places or objects change.

Research details
How it worksAccumulate a spatiotemporal environment and robot feature map to condition mobile manipulation over extended tasks.
Why it mattersCurrent-frame policies omit spatial history that matters when navigating between later manipulation subgoals.
Open questionHow is stale map content corrected after objects move or the robot revisits a scene?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Articulated 3D Scene Graphs

Articulated 3D Scene Graphs uses observed object interactions to estimate how doors, drawers and other articulated objects can move. The system builds a semantic and kinematic scene graph from RGB-D observations, then uses that structure to execute language-specified mobile manipulation tasks. It combines object identity with executable articulation knowledge rather than relying on a static scene map.

Research details
How it worksInfer articulation kinematics and semantics from object interactions, then use a semantic-kinematic scene graph for mobile manipulation.
Why it mattersA scene graph becomes useful for action when it includes how a door or drawer can actually move.
Open questionHow does the graph handle unseen articulation types or an object whose behavior changes after contact?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

RAM reachability

RAM predicts whether a robot morphology can reach a requested 3D pose, without solving full inverse kinematics each time. A morphology encoder conditions a learned reachability representation trained on many robot geometries. This supports faster workspace queries and gradient-based morphology optimization when the question is feasibility, not an explicit joint configuration.

Research details
How it worksCondition a learned reachability representation on robot morphology to answer pose-feasibility queries without repeatedly solving full inverse kinematics.
Why it mattersMany design and workspace queries need to know whether a solution exists rather than the exact joint configuration.
Open questionHow are false-positive reachability predictions checked before physical execution?

Day 2 · Spotlight paper

Shape Your Body

Shape Your Body jointly considers learned locomotion capability and robot hardware design. After training a generalist controller and critic across varied morphologies, the system uses gradients through the frozen value function to improve embodiment parameters. It proposes an efficient alternative to repeatedly retraining a separate controller for each candidate robot design.

Research details
How it worksTrain a shared controller and critic across morphologies, freeze them and use value gradients to improve design parameters.
Why it mattersHardware design can reuse learned control knowledge rather than retraining a policy for every proposed body.
Open questionAre optimized bodies mechanically feasible, and does the frozen critic remain trustworthy outside its training morphologies?

Tesla

Tesla describes how it uses learned world models and counterfactual simulation to test robustness under unusual driving and robotics scenarios. The presentation emphasizes predicting the consequences of events that may be rare or unsafe to stage physically, then checking how learned policies respond. The speaker explicitly says the talk does not provide detailed new Optimus-policy results; product claims are attributable to Tesla.

How it worksUse learned world models and counterfactual simulation to test policies on rare or difficult physical scenarios.
Why it mattersRealistic-looking generated events are useful only if they reveal genuine policy failure modes.

Day 3 · Debate

Commercially Viable Generalist Robots — Special Debate

An explicit debate about whether large-scale behavior cloning and in-domain improvement are enough for commercially useful generalist robots. Arguments cover how to define generality, the economic cost of physical data, real-world reliability, simulation, hierarchy and inference-time computation. Debate sides were assigned by the moderator and should not be treated as fixed personal positions.

Research details
How it worksDebate generality, commercial economics, physical data cost, behavior cloning, inference-time reasoning and alternative system designs.
Why it mattersDifferent definitions of generality and acceptable reliability can make apparently opposed arguments hard to compare.
Open questionWhat observable deployment would distinguish the competing claims, and under which definition of a generalist robot?

FAR: Failure-Aware Retry for Test-Time Recovery and Continual Policy Improvement

Haoran Hao, Shahram Najam Syed, Jeffrey Ichnowski, Jeff Schneider

Primary paper reviewed

FAR addresses the case in which an existing diffusion policy fails and a naive retry repeats the same behavior. It uses critic estimates to select potentially failure-inducing action chunks, pairs them with higher-valued alternatives, and performs a short preference-based policy update before retrying. Smoothed action perturbations provide local exploration. A separate improvement loop combines expert data, successful online trajectories and failed trajectories: the critic learns from the collected experience, while the actor learns from expert and successful data. The reported evaluation covers nine simulated manipulation tasks and three real xArm tasks, with bounded retry budgets. The paper supports distinguishing immediate recovery from longer-term policy improvement, but its autonomy claim needs care: real experiments use a human’s binary success/failure signal, and the arm is returned to its initial configuration between retries while the scene remains changed. Tests use single-task diffusion policies trained from scratch; transfer to large pretrained VLAs and principled automatic failure detection are stated future work.

Research details
How it worksUse critic estimates to select failure chunks, update the diffusion policy from failure/alternative preferences, and retry with smoothed perturbations. Replay recovery experience for further training.
Why it mattersSeparates immediate retry adaptation from later learning, while exposing human outcome signals and partial resets as part of the tested workflow.
Open questionDo recovery gains survive automatic failure detection, safety-constrained exploration and transfer to large pretrained policies?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗Manuscript ↗arXiv ↗Project ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary manuscript main text, method (§4), experiments (§5), limitations (§6), and evaluation protocol (§C.3) read through the supported PDF-text reader; primary project page also read. Other appendix sections were not comprehensively reviewed. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The real-world protocol depends on a human-provided binary outcome signal; FAR does not supply a principled autonomous failure detector.

Retries still return the arm to an initial configuration. Avoiding full scene resets is different from eliminating every intervention.

The evaluated policies are trained from scratch in single-task settings; no demonstrated universal transfer to generalist VLAs.

Recovery exploration safety remains future work, and reported success is measured under finite retry budgets.

ImageWAM: Do World Action Models Really Need Video Generation, or Just Image Editing?

Yuyang Zhang, Wenyao Zhang, Zekun Qi, He Zhang, Haitao Lin, Jingbo Zhang, Yao Mu, Xiaokang Yang, Wenjun Zeng, Xin Jin

Primary paper reviewed

ImageWAM attaches an action expert to an image-editing backbone. During inference it computes editing-aware attention context from one editing-branch step, then denoises an action chunk using that context. It does not decode a complete future image or generate a dense future video for each update. The study reports simulation benchmarks and four dual-arm hardware tasks, with multiple editing backbones. This supports examining how much visual prediction an action policy needs in those settings, rather than declaring video prediction unnecessary for all robot control.

Research details
How it worksTrain the editing branch and action expert together, retain frozen understanding components, and use editing caches to condition action flow matching.
Why it mattersSupplies a main-paper alternative to dense future-video intermediates and separates one editing-step shortcut from the remaining action-denoising computation.
Open questionWhich dynamic or longer-horizon tasks require temporal prediction that an editing-cache intermediate does not retain?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗Manuscript ↗arXiv ↗Project ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed manuscript architecture, objectives, inference, experiments and ablations, corroborated by the complete primary project page. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

A single editing-branch step is not a single-step action-generation or complete-control-loop guarantee.

Reported results cover the specified training, benchmark and hardware settings; generalized dominance is not established.

Different backbone variants and efficiency baselines use different interfaces, so figures should not be pooled without their protocols.

Compact inference: “At test time, ImageWAM uses one editing forward step and internal KV caches, avoiding dense future-video denoising and decoding.” Source ↗

LaWAM: Latent World Action Models for Efficient Dynamics-Aware Robot Policies

Jialei Chen, Kai Wang, Kang Chen, Shuaihang Chen, Feng Gao, Wenhao Tang, Zhiyuan Li, Weilin Liu, Zhuyu Yao, Boxun Li, Yuanbo Xu, Chao Yu

Primary paper reviewed

LaWAM learns a latent-action-conditioned world model in a frozen visual feature space, then teaches a language-conditioned policy to predict the latent action needed for a future subgoal. An action expert uses that compact future feature without rendering future pixels. The manuscript includes physical-time alignment for mixed-frequency action data and controlled task evaluations. Its stated limitations include unstable camera motion and insufficient coverage of fine deformable dynamics. Coherent open-loop latent rollouts on other embodiments are not the same evidence as successful closed-loop control on a new robot.

Research details
How it worksPretrain latent dynamics, distill transition codes into a policy prior, and condition action chunks on a predicted latent visual subgoal.
Why it mattersConnects predictive representation design with practical action timing, while identifying where future-state features and native action frequencies enter the policy.
Open questionCan its latent dynamics retain useful task change when camera self-motion or fine contact deformation dominates the observation?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗Manuscript ↗arXiv ↗Project ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed manuscript model stages, component ablations, physical-time alignment, real-robot protocols and limitations, corroborated by the complete primary project page. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The paper states a preference for relatively stable camera views and weaker modeling of rare fine-grained deformation.

Open-loop cross-embodiment latent visualization does not establish zero-shot closed-loop policy deployment on those robots.

The project page includes additional evaluations; they are not pooled with the retrieved manuscript protocol or other papers’ timing measurements.

Limitations: “LaWAM is currently most effective in manipulation settings with relatively stable camera views.” Source ↗

Physical-Time Alignment for Mixed-Frequency Data: “the same action-token index does not necessarily represent the same elapsed physical time.” Source ↗

Scale Up Strategically: Learning Compositional Generalization via Bias-Aware Evaluation and Data Collection for Robotic Manipulation

Yu Qi, Zhang Ye, Xinyi Xu, Yuxuan Lu, Amitoj Sandhu, Boce Hu, Haojie Huang, Jonathan Tremblay, Lawson L.S. Wong

Primary paper reviewed

This study asks how a fixed demonstration budget should be distributed across instruction factors, rather than treating data scale as a single count. It deliberately correlates pairs of factors during fine-tuning, then evaluates held-out combinations to diagnose which factor a policy follows when cues conflict. A vision-language judge supplies factor-level failure labels. The authors use those diagnostics to collect more informative combinations under matched demonstration and configuration-change budgets. Their simulation and real-robot studies report benefits from this targeted allocation, but the appendix also identifies settings where the advantage disappears, particularly difficult size distinctions. The contribution is a concrete data-selection perspective: first identify an under-grounded capability, then test whether reallocating examples helps it. The reported hierarchy and improvements are scoped to the tested policies, task factors and collection protocols.

Research details
How it worksDiagnose instruction-factor shortcuts, then allocate a fixed demonstration and scene-change budget to under-grounded factors.
Why it mattersMore data can preserve the same shortcut; useful demonstrations should target the capability that is missing.
Open questionDoes targeted collection still help when tasks and language are less structured than the tested factor grids?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗Manuscript ↗arXiv ↗Project ↗Code ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed primary manuscript methodological appendix, factor-bias evaluation, collection strategies and experiments; author project page methods/results also read. Indexed formulas and some table values are malformed, so numerical claims are not reproduced here. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The tested instruction factors and structured task grids do not cover arbitrary open-world language or manipulation.

Failure attribution relies on a VLM judge; its agreement with human labels is checked on a subset, not established universally.

Some reported size-related settings show little collection-strategy benefit.

Collection cost includes configuration changes, so claims should preserve both the demonstration budget and the scene-change budget.

Factor-change counting per strategy: “fix the total factor change f and the budget” Source ↗

ContactGuard: Pre-Contact Execution Monitoring with Action-Conditioned Latent World Models

Gehan Zheng, Matthew Johnson-Roberson, Weiming Zhi

Primary paper reviewed

ContactGuard is an execution monitor for a policy that proposes action chunks. It learns action-conditioned visual dynamics from unlabeled robot trajectories, freezes that latent world model, and trains a small failure probe on labeled pre-contact clips. Before a predicted gripper closure, the monitor rolls the model forward under the policy’s own planned actions and scores the future latent. A task-calibrated threshold can veto the chunk while the underlying policy remains unchanged. The experiments use four grasp settings on a dual-arm robot and compare future-latent monitoring against matched current-state and action-corruption controls. The live evaluation is a controlled counterfactual protocol: flagged attempts pause before contact and then resume so the would-be outcome can be recorded. Its claim is predictive abstention, not completed autonomous recovery or policy learning. The paper explicitly leaves post-abort completion and longer-horizon monitoring for future work. It therefore supports reporting false aborts, missed failures and subsequent task completion separately.

Research details
How it worksRoll a frozen latent world model forward under the proposed action chunk; a trained failure probe can veto imminent contact.
Why it mattersPre-contact detection is separate from recovery: the published monitor abstains but does not finish the task after an abort.
Open questionCan calibration hold on new contacts while a recovery module completes vetoed tasks at an acceptable false-abort rate?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗Manuscript ↗arXiv ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed primary manuscript introduction, latent-model/probe methods, online monitor, experimental setup/results and limitations read. Figures and the complete original PDF were not independently inspected. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

It abstains but does not repair the scene or complete the task after an abort.

The implemented trigger is an imminent commanded gripper closure; general contact-event triggering is not demonstrated.

Evaluation covers four grasp settings and per-task validation thresholds, not arbitrary long-horizon skills.

The live protocol pauses and resumes flagged chunks to label counterfactual outcomes; it is not an evaluation of a complete abort-and-recover system.

Conclusions, Limitations, and Future Work: “ContactGuard prevents failures by abstaining, but does not recover from them or complete the task after an abort.” Source ↗

Imitation from Heterogeneous Demonstrations using Grounded Latent-Action World Models

Tianyou Wang, Anson Lei, Joe Watson, Ingmar Posner

Primary paper reviewed

GLAM learns a shared latent-action representation from target robot demonstrations and cheaper auxiliary trajectories that need not carry executable action labels. One model infers latent actions from visual transitions; another uses target action labels to make those latents decodable into robot control. An asymmetric alignment loss transfers the target branch’s control information into the transition-based representation. The resulting model relabels heterogeneous trajectories for a downstream imitation policy. The authors test Kinova robot data and a simulated floating-UMI-gripper source, with an object-mask variant to emphasize manipulated-object motion. They report data-efficiency gains and useful auxiliary-data scaling in these settings. This is evidence for control-grounded representation as an alternative to simply sharing raw action coordinates. It is not demonstrated web-video or human-hand transfer: the source and target share scenes, camera placement, objects and task semantics, and tactile or force information is absent.

Research details
How it worksAlign transition-inferred latents with target-action-supervised latents, then train from labeled robot and unlabeled auxiliary trajectories in the shared representation.
Why it mattersAuxiliary experience can teach usable control without already matching the target robot’s raw action interface.
Open questionCan the latent bridge handle different viewpoints, task semantics, dexterous hands, and contact feedback absent from the tested sources?

Max Du, Zhanyi Sun, Chen Xu, Paarth Shah, Masha Itkina, Shuran Song

Primary project reviewed

Memory Anchors studies which old experiences help a robot policy retain earlier tasks during sequential learning. It identifies new-task observations that overlap old-task representations but require different actions, then selects nearby old experiences for replay. For diffusion policies, the project measures action disagreement through conditional denoising to reduce confusion from multiple valid action modes. Controlled experiments remove or enrich these anchors while keeping the replay budget comparable, and the authors report changes in forgetting in simulation and diagnostic real-robot task sequences. The project also emphasizes that replay cannot consist only of high-conflict anchors: diverse old experience remains important. This is persistent policy training from selected past data, not inference-time conversational memory. Extracting anchors needs the model’s representation space and past training data; the evaluated task sequences and robots do not establish unlimited continual deployment.

Research details
How it worksIdentify overlapping old/new states with conflicting actions, select nearby old experiences, and mix these anchors with diverse replay during training.
Why it mattersReplay composition can matter beyond buffer size; important old decision states help protect previous skills.
Open questionCan anchor selection work with inaccessible pretraining data, very large histories, and longer task sequences without losing replay diversity?

Author project page methods, controlled replay experiments, real-robot examples and limitations read (source reader L0–546), plus indexed manuscript abstract and conclusion. Full indexed manuscript methods were unavailable. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Finding anchors requires access to model representations and past data.

Computing representations scales with dataset history and may need approximation.

Anchors alone reduce replay diversity; they are not a replacement for all other old data.

The manuscript discusses relatively short task sequences; real-world examples are controlled diagnostic tasks.

The reviewed project and indexed abstract/conclusion support these notes, but the full manuscript methods were not retrieved.

Multisensory Continual Learning: Adapting Pretrained Visuomotor Policies to Force

Jaden Clark, Changhao Wang, Yihuai Gao, Seongheon Hong, Hojung Choi, Mark Cutkosky, Yifan Hou, Shuran Song

Primary paper reviewed

MuSe asks how a policy pretrained without a sensor can acquire that modality later while preserving its earlier capabilities. The studied case adds force-torque sensing to a pretrained Unified Video-Action model. Early token fusion and later cross-attention adapters combine the sensor with vision and other inputs; the model predicts future observations, force-torque signals and actions. During adaptation, replay mixes the original pretraining data with new multisensory demonstrations, masking the force input and force loss where those measurements are absent. The evaluation separates force prediction on previously unsupervised tasks, forward transfer to new contact-rich tasks and backward transfer to pretraining tasks. The authors report improvements in their tabletop settings, while no-replay ablations exhibit substantial forgetting. This is evidence for a particular sensor-expansion and replay strategy, not a result that every added sensor improves every policy. Only force-torque expansion, limited tasks and access to the original pretraining data were tested; broader modalities, embodiments and longer horizons remain future work.

Research details
How it worksAdd force-torque fusion and future prediction to pretrained UVA; mix new multisensory demonstrations with original-data replay, masking absent force inputs and losses.
Why it mattersSeparates new-sensor adaptation, old-task retention and cross-modal transfer; the tested case adds force-torque sensing.
Open questionWill retention hold without stored pretraining data, or when adding touch, audio or depth instead of force-torque?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗Manuscript ↗arXiv ↗Project ↗

HARBOR: A Harness Framework for Agentic Robot Reinforcement Learning

Zechu Li, Yufeng Jin, Xiao-Yang Liu, Puze Liu, Vignesh Prasad, Carlo D'Eramo, Georgia Chalvatzaki

Primary paper reviewed

HARBOR automates the engineering workflow surrounding robot reinforcement learning in simulation. A central agent divides a request into bounded stages such as dependencies, task construction, rewards, domain randomization, RL integration and tuning. Stage-local agents operate through standard commands and persistent artifacts. Executable gates check interfaces and rollout evidence before later stages proceed; failures are repaired within a retry budget and unresolved stages can require human intervention. Reward and hyperparameter candidates run in isolated parallel trials, while an experience ledger preserves useful heuristics and failure diagnoses for later runs. This separates the coding agent that constructs or tunes the experiment from the numerical RL algorithm that trains the policy. The authors evaluate multiple simulation backends and include physical validation, but the latter uses user-provided real trajectories, interface engineering and human feedback for simulator alignment. The source explicitly warns that gates do not guarantee semantic policy correctness. Its results support a scoped engineering-automation claim, not a general guarantee that any agent can autonomously train reliable real-world policies.

Research details
How it worksStage-specific agents build simulation tasks, rewards and training configurations; executable gates check artifacts, parallel RL trials compare candidates, and experience ledgers preserve useful engineering lessons.
Why it mattersSeparates the agent’s engineering decisions from RL’s parameter updates and makes intermediate evidence inspectable.
Open questionHow much prior scaffolding and human engineering remains necessary for unfamiliar tasks and real-robot transfer?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗Manuscript ↗arXiv ↗Project ↗Code ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed manuscript main methods, experiments, real-world validation, ablations and stated limitations were read. Primary project guide was also read to corroborate the harness design. Indexed equations/tables contain formatting loss, so extracted table values are not used for headline comparisons; appendices were not reviewed exhaustively. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Executable gates catch particular engineering failures but do not prove that the reward captures the intended behavior or that the final policy is semantically correct.

The authors explicitly retain manual robot-interface engineering, user-provided real trajectories and human feedback at the sim-to-real boundary.

The evaluated policies are relatively simple; extending the framework to VLA or world-model policies is described as future work.

Some reward-design gains rely on supplied human heuristics and accumulated experience. Their contribution should remain visible when comparing automation methods.

Harness Abstractions for RL: “HARBOR does not guarantee semantic correctness of the final policy.” Source ↗

Parallel Tuning with Experience Learning: “after each tuning round, the main agent distills recurring patterns across trials into short bullet points” Source ↗

Limitations and Future Work: “deployment to physical robots still requires manual engineering around robot interfaces and human feedback.” Source ↗

ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World

Wenli Xiao, Jia Xie, Tonghe Zhang, Haotian Lin, Letian Fu, Haoru Xue, Jalen Lu, Yi Yang, Cunxi Dai, Zi Wang, Jimmy Wu, Guanzhi Wang, S. Shankar Sastry, Ken Goldberg, Linxi Fan, Yuke Zhu, Guanya Shi

Primary project reviewed

ENPIRE makes selected physical manipulation tasks accessible to coding agents as repeatable research environments. Its Environment component resets scenes and verifies outcomes; Policy Improvement launches a chosen refinement routine; Rollout evaluates candidates on one or more robots; Evolution lets coding agents inspect failures and modify algorithm or infrastructure code. The improvement interface accepts several regimes, including heuristics, code/tool use, behavior cloning, offline RL and online RL. Consequently, the changed artifact can be an executable program, a training recipe or a learned policy, depending on the experiment. The project describes agent-run iterations on prepared tasks such as Push-T and pin insertion, together with simulation experiments and fleet-resource measurements. This is evidence of an engineered loop around real interaction, rather than merely a supervisor choosing skills during one episode. Its autonomy claim is scoped to the provided self-resetting, self-verifying task interfaces. The site labels its showcased 99% result as pass@8, so it should not be rewritten as single-attempt reliability. All results remain author-reported.

Research details
How it worksCoding agents propose policy or training-code changes, run selectable refinement routines, and evaluate real rollouts through a task-specific automatic reset and verification harness.
Why it mattersMakes code changes and RL-based policy updates available within one physical experiment loop, while exposing setup and resource costs.
Open questionHow well does it work with imperfect resets or reward verification, and how much effort is needed to prepare a new task environment?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗Manuscript ↗arXiv ↗Project ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

The indexed manuscript yielded only title/abstract. The complete primary project page was read, including the four-module method, physical reset/evaluation examples, policy-improvement regimes, fleet experiments and stated limitations. Full manuscript methods were not available through the indexed reader. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The demonstrated autonomy assumes task-specific automatic reset, perception, reward verification and available robot-control tools; it is not evidence of autonomous setup for arbitrary robots or tasks.

The primary page reports 99% pass@8 on showcased tasks. That metric permits repeated attempts and is not a single-rollout success guarantee.

The authors report robot underutilization while agents read, debug or wait, and rising token consumption as fleets and coordinating agents scale.

This review used substantive primary project text plus an indexed abstract, not a complete primary manuscript-method review.

Abstract / L33–35: “Coding agents can improve policies with various PI regimes, such as heuristic learning, tool calling, behavior cloning, offline or online RL.” Source ↗

Learned Manipulation Policy / L40: “Policies trained with ENPIRE reach a 99% pass@8 success rate across the showcased manipulation tasks.” Source ↗

From Robot Hardware to an Agent-Operable Environment / L153–154: “Before an agent can improve a robot policy, the task must become self-resetting and self-verifying.” Source ↗

MobiAgent: Dual-Loop Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation

Chenzhi Liu, Yue Zhang, Jiehong Lin, Jianan Wang, Bo Wang, Zhongrui Wang, Xiaojuan Qi

Primary paper reviewed

MobiAgent separates deployment-time planning from offline policy refinement. Its inner loop uses a VLM planner, a shared VLM trunk with skill-specific flow-matching action experts, and a reflection critic that recommends advance, retry or replan. Critic observations are retained as episode memory. The outer loop runs after episode termination: it segments and verifies trajectories, standardizes skill captions and trains or fine-tunes neural skill policies. Startup data creates the skill inventory; subsequent rollout data is assigned to the existing inventory, and the described continual phase updates those existing policies without expanding the model inventory. This is more specific than saying the robot simply learns through reasoning or that its skill vocabulary grows without bound. The authors report finite deployment-to-training rounds on RoboCasa and Astribot S1, plus long-horizon BEHAVIOR tasks. Early RoboCasa gains later plateau. Here the reusable changes are learned skill policies and curated data; the paper does not establish indefinite improvement or a learning procedure that recursively redesigns itself.

Research details
How it worksAn online planner and critic compose learned skills; after episodes, verified rollout clips fine-tune the existing skill policies offline.
Why it mattersDistinguishes execution-time memory from later parameter learning using deployment data.
Open questionDo updates retain older skills, and can the system handle behavior outside its startup skill inventory?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗Manuscript ↗arXiv ↗Project ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary manuscript introduction, inner/outer-loop methods, main experiments and conclusion/limitations were read, together with the complete primary project page and reported deployment-round tables. Detailed supplementary prompts and all appendix failure cases were not exhaustively reviewed. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Continuous rollout refinement updates the existing skill-policy inventory; startup skill discovery should not be rewritten as unrestricted discovery of new skills during every deployment round.

The authors identify interference with earlier behaviors, pose-correction churn, critic drift and visual occlusion as remaining problems.

Reported RoboCasa gains plateau in later rounds, and the real-robot improvement covers four tasks and two update rounds rather than unbounded lifelong learning.

The title’s recursive self-improvement claim concerns repeated deployment-data recycling and policy training; the reviewed experiments do not establish improvement of the training procedure itself.

ATOM-Bench: A Real-World Benchmark for Atomic Skills and Compositional Generalization in Manipulation Policies

Zenan Wu, Bingqing Wei, Lu Liu, Zheqi He, Wang Xi, liujiakang, lizehui, Guocai Yao, Jing-Shu Zheng, Xi Yang, Yongtao Wang

Primary project reviewed

ATOM-Bench separates learning elementary manipulation skills from recombining them under new task structures. Its motor set isolates physical operations, its instruction set isolates language constraints, and a held-out composition set combines those factors. Models are adapted on atomic tasks only, rather than being shown demonstrations of the compositional test tasks. The project describes paired single-arm Franka Panda and dual-arm Cobot Magic tracks, with fixed physical test seeds and metrics for task completion, partial progress and composition failures. The reported models often perform much better on atomic tasks than on held-out combinations. This is useful evidence for asking what a benchmark score actually measures: a successful familiar operation is not automatically evidence of compositional reuse. The scope remains tabletop manipulation on these platforms and these adaptation protocols, not general home or factory performance. The project page reports results for its selected policies; it does not establish that every VLA has the same failure profile.

Research details
How it worksFine-tune on atomic motor and instruction tasks, then test held-out compositions on two robot platforms using fixed physical seeds.
Why it mattersSeparates familiar skill execution from recombining skills; results remain scoped to the benchmark’s tasks, platforms and adaptation recipe.
Open questionHow stable are compositional results under more seeds, different adaptation budgets and tasks beyond tabletop manipulation?

Scope, limitations & sources

Complete primary project page read, including task factorization, real-robot platforms, adaptation/test protocol and static results. The indexed-paper reader did not contain this ID; the full manuscript was not read. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Results are conditioned on the particular atomic-to-compositional split and the two hardware tracks.

Ten fixed physical seeds improve reproducibility but do not represent the full deployment distribution.

The displayed model comparisons concern the listed versions and training recipe; they cannot be generalized to all newer policies.

The complete primary project page was reviewed, not the full manuscript or an independent replication.

H2RBench: A Real-to-Sim Benchmark for Evaluating Human-to-Robot Transfer

Chuyang Xiao, Haotian Zhan, Sriram Krishna, Peilin Meng, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Sergey Zakharov, David Held

Primary paper reviewed

H2RBench compares human-to-robot transfer methods under a shared task and supervision protocol. It reconstructs real workspaces in simulation, uses real human demonstrations, and holds the robot-demonstration budget fixed while varying the amount of human data. The evaluated methods bridge embodiments through visual editing, keypoints, latent dynamics or hierarchical subgoals. The reported human-data benefit varies by method and task: it is more consistent for coarse spatial behavior than for precise contact and longer sequences, and adding human data can hurt insertion performance. The benchmark also compares rankings from separately trained simulation-pipeline and real-world-pipeline policies. That correspondence supports comparative evaluation in the tested setup; it does not show that a single simulated policy transfers unchanged to arbitrary real settings. The task suite remains limited to controlled third-person tabletop manipulation, primarily with rigid objects.

Research details
How it worksHold robot-data budgets fixed, vary human demonstrations, compare transfer methods on shared tasks, and check simulated versus real-world rankings.
Why it mattersSeparates human-data scaling from robot supervision and exposes precision and long-horizon bottlenecks.
Open questionDo the scaling trends and simulated rankings hold for egocentric, deformable, articulated, bimanual, or in-the-wild tasks?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗Manuscript ↗arXiv ↗Project ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed primary manuscript: problem definition, task suite, reconstruction/data collection, method interfaces, evaluation/scaling, sim-versus-real validation, limitations and implementation/failure analyses. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Four controlled tabletop tasks and limited interaction families.

Real-to-sim reconstruction has imperfect visual and physical fidelity.

Simulation and real-world comparisons use separately trained policies; this is not zero-shot transfer of one checkpoint.

Method–task interactions, especially contact-sensitive stacking, account for remaining ranking discrepancies.

Overview: “we hold the robot demonstration budget fixed across methods” Source ↗

Workshop paper · Do Robots Need World Models? A Debate on Dynamics Learning, Planning, and End-to-End Robot Learning

LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs

Primary paper reviewed

LeWAM jointly learns action-conditioned latent dynamics and a flow-matching action policy. It can sample actions directly or refine candidate plans by differentiating through the learned dynamics. Its goal-image planning experiments and goal-free behavior-cloning experiments test different uses of that model family. The physical-robot experiments use direct policy execution; they do not demonstrate that online planning improves every physical task. Models are trained or adapted for individual tasks and embodiments.

Research details
How it worksJointly train latent-state prediction and action generation; for planning, refine sampled action sequences while holding model parameters fixed.
Why it mattersProvides a concrete way to investigate direct execution and explicit prediction-based planning within a related model family, while making the evaluation setting explicit.
Open questionDoes the planning benefit survive unfamiliar objects, changing viewpoints and real-robot goal-conditioned tasks at a matched runtime budget?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed manuscript methods, evaluation protocols, physical-robot experiments and limitations, cross-checked against the primary arXiv abstract and HTML introduction. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Physical-robot results use direct execution, while visual planning has goal images and a separate evaluation protocol.

Tasks and embodiments are trained or adapted separately; broad multitask transfer is a proposed extension.

Data coverage, longer horizons and larger candidate populations remain scaling questions.

The organizers list the same full title. The accepted OpenReview version and author list were not exposed by that listing, so the reviewed arXiv version is identified separately.

LeWAM Planning: “During refinement, model parameters remain frozen and only the normalized action plans receive gradients.” Source ↗

Conclusion and Limitations: “Models are trained or adapted separately for each task and embodiment.” Source ↗

Workshop paper · Do Robots Need World Models? A Debate on Dynamics Learning, Planning, and End-to-End Robot Learning

Rolling-WAM: World Action Models with Rolling Imagination

Primary paper reviewed

Rolling-WAM distributes joint video-action denoising across successive control updates. It completes the next action chunk while retaining partially refined future chunks, then incorporates a new observation as the window advances. The paper evaluates simulation benchmarks and three Unitree G1 manipulation tasks. Its timing comparison measures steady-state replanning rather than startup or the complete robot lifecycle. The authors also identify a trade-off: retained future predictions can lag behind rapid scene changes, particularly with long windows.

Research details
How it worksMaintain a sliding video-action prediction window at staggered noise levels; finish, execute and replace the nearest chunk while refining its future continuation.
Why it mattersChanges how prediction compute is allocated over time, supplying another concrete timing strategy alongside the conference discussion of robot control clocks.
Open questionHow do window size and initialization cost affect response to abrupt changes outside the demonstrated task distribution?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed manuscript methods, training, benchmark protocols, real-robot evaluation and limitations, corroborated by the primary project page. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Latency timing includes visual encoding and denoising but excludes warm-up and initialization.

The physical evaluation covers three manipulation tasks; it is not evidence of unrestricted humanoid generality.

Long prediction windows can preserve stale future context.

Title and first author match the Efficient Foundation Models workshop listing. The world-model workshop separately lists it as website-only; accepted versions are not assumed identical.

Inference Efficiency: “Timing includes visual encoding and denoising, with CUDA synchronization, and excludes warm-up and initialization.” Source ↗

Conclusion: limitations: “Despite observation feedback, retained predictions may lag behind rapid scene changes and misguide action generation, particularly with long windows.” Source ↗
