Workshop paper · Efficient Foundation Models for Real-Time Embodied AI

Rolling-WAM: World Action Models with Rolling Imagination

Yinghua Zhou et al.

Primary paper reviewed

Rolling-WAM distributes joint video-action denoising across successive control updates. It completes the next action chunk while retaining partially refined future chunks, then incorporates a new observation as the window advances. The paper evaluates simulation benchmarks and three Unitree G1 manipulation tasks. Its timing comparison measures steady-state replanning rather than startup or the complete robot lifecycle. The authors also identify a trade-off: retained future predictions can lag behind rapid scene changes, particularly with long windows.

Research details
How it worksMaintain a sliding video-action prediction window at staggered noise levels; finish, execute and replace the nearest chunk while refining its future continuation.
Why it mattersChanges how prediction compute is allocated over time, supplying another concrete timing strategy alongside the conference discussion of robot control clocks.
Open questionHow do window size and initialization cost affect response to abrupt changes outside the demonstrated task distribution?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed manuscript methods, training, benchmark protocols, real-robot evaluation and limitations, corroborated by the primary project page. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Latency timing includes visual encoding and denoising but excludes warm-up and initialization.

The physical evaluation covers three manipulation tasks; it is not evidence of unrestricted humanoid generality.

Long prediction windows can preserve stale future context.

Title and first author match the Efficient Foundation Models workshop listing. The world-model workshop separately lists it as website-only; accepted versions are not assumed identical.

Inference Efficiency: “Timing includes visual encoding and denoising, with CUDA synchronization, and excludes warm-up and initialization.” Source ↗

Conclusion: limitations: “Despite observation feedback, retained predictions may lag behind rapid scene changes and misguide action generation, particularly with long windows.” Source ↗

Workshop paper · Pretrain to Adapt: What Makes a Pretrained Policy Adaptable?

Multisensory Continual Learning: Adapting Pretrained Visuomotor Policies to Force

Jaden Clark, Changhao Wang, Yihuai Gao, Seongheon Hong, Hojung Choi, Mark Cutkosky, Yifan Hou, Shuran Song

Primary paper reviewed

MuSe asks how a policy pretrained without a sensor can acquire that modality later while preserving its earlier capabilities. The studied case adds force-torque sensing to a pretrained Unified Video-Action model. Early token fusion and later cross-attention adapters combine the sensor with vision and other inputs; the model predicts future observations, force-torque signals and actions. During adaptation, replay mixes the original pretraining data with new multisensory demonstrations, masking the force input and force loss where those measurements are absent. The evaluation separates force prediction on previously unsupervised tasks, forward transfer to new contact-rich tasks and backward transfer to pretraining tasks. The authors report improvements in their tabletop settings, while no-replay ablations exhibit substantial forgetting. This is evidence for a particular sensor-expansion and replay strategy, not a result that every added sensor improves every policy. Only force-torque expansion, limited tasks and access to the original pretraining data were tested; broader modalities, embodiments and longer horizons remain future work.

Research details
How it worksAdd force-torque fusion and future prediction to pretrained UVA; mix new multisensory demonstrations with original-data replay, masking absent force inputs and losses.
Why it mattersSeparates new-sensor adaptation, old-task retention and cross-modal transfer; the tested case adds force-torque sensing.
Open questionWill retention hold without stored pretraining data, or when adding touch, audio or depth instead of force-torque?
Reviewed primary source ↗Organizer listing ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary v4 HTML manuscript main text (§1–5), methods, force-torque case study, ablations and limitations read. References and appendices were not comprehensively reviewed. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The demonstrated sensor-expansion case is force-torque; other modalities and combinations are untested.

Replay assumes access to the original pretraining data.

The real-world evaluation is a limited tabletop task set; diverse robots and longer-horizon tasks remain future work.

Some reported task scores use partial credit, so fractional totals should not be described as counts of independently successful trials.

§5 Limitations and future works, lines 307–311: “We study multi-sensory continual learning through a single sensor-expansion case: adding force–torque sensing to a pretrained vision-action policy.” Source ↗

Workshop paper · Pretrain to Adapt: What Makes a Pretrained Policy Adaptable?

Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning

Maximilian Du, Zhanyi Sun, Chen Xu, Paarth Shah, Masha Itkina, Shuran Song

Primary project reviewed

Memory Anchors studies which old experiences help a robot policy retain earlier tasks during sequential learning. It identifies new-task observations that overlap old-task representations but require different actions, then selects nearby old experiences for replay. For diffusion policies, the project measures action disagreement through conditional denoising to reduce confusion from multiple valid action modes. Controlled experiments remove or enrich these anchors while keeping the replay budget comparable, and the authors report changes in forgetting in simulation and diagnostic real-robot task sequences. The project also emphasizes that replay cannot consist only of high-conflict anchors: diverse old experience remains important. This is persistent policy training from selected past data, not inference-time conversational memory. Extracting anchors needs the model’s representation space and past training data; the evaluated task sequences and robots do not establish unlimited continual deployment.

Research details
How it worksIdentify overlapping old/new states with conflicting actions, select nearby old experiences, and mix these anchors with diverse replay during training.
Why it mattersReplay composition can matter beyond buffer size; important old decision states help protect previous skills.
Open questionCan anchor selection work with inaccessible pretraining data, very large histories, and longer task sequences without losing replay diversity?
Reviewed primary source ↗Organizer listing ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Author project page methods, controlled replay experiments, real-robot examples and limitations read (source reader L0–546), plus indexed manuscript abstract and conclusion. Full indexed manuscript methods were unavailable. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Finding anchors requires access to model representations and past data.

Computing representations scales with dataset history and may need approximation.

Anchors alone reduce replay diversity; they are not a replacement for all other old data.

The manuscript discusses relatively short task sequences; real-world examples are controlled diagnostic tasks.

The reviewed project and indexed abstract/conclusion support these notes, but the full manuscript methods were not retrieved.

Adding More Memory Anchors / Why not use all Memory Anchors? (L311–315): “Having high buffer diversity is also important” Source ↗

Workshop paper · Pretrain to Adapt: What Makes a Pretrained Policy Adaptable?

RARA: Robust Policy Fine-Tuning through Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment for Robotic Manipulation

Xuhui Kang, Sung-Wook Lee, Yan Zhuang, Tianle Zhong, Yen-Ling Kuo

Primary paper reviewed

RARA reuses selected pretraining demonstrations to guide task adaptation. It retrieves trajectories by instruction similarity, then matches target frames to relevant source phases by action-chunk similarity. First it trains representation-producing layers and a small projector to align target features with frozen pretrained features. It then behavior-clones the target task while constraining how the policy represents the retrieved source observations. Retrieved source actions form alignment pairs; they are not extra behavior-cloning targets. In the reported diffusion-policy and GR00T experiments, this combination improves adaptation under visual shifts. Data choice is crucial: using unrelated pretraining skills or random pairings can remove the gain and sometimes hurt performance. The method therefore supplies a selection-and-preservation perspective on post-training, rather than a claim that anchoring any prior representation is beneficial. The experiments keep the robot and action space fixed and require relevant pretraining data.

Research details
How it worksRetrieve relevant pretraining trajectories, align target features to their pretrained features, then fine-tune while anchoring source representations.
Why it mattersUseful prior data can preserve representations; unrelated reference skills can instead harm adaptation.
Open questionHow can suitable anchors be found without related pretraining data, or when embodiment and action space change?
Reviewed primary source ↗Organizer listing ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed primary manuscript problem definition, retrieval/two-stage objectives, model and environment setup, ID/OOD evaluation, component/data ablations, conclusion and relevant-data limitations. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Relevant pretraining data must contain the same type of skill as the target.

Tests focus on visual shifts with the same robot and action space, not cross-embodiment transfer.

RARA adds a representation-alignment stage before the ordinary fine-tuning budget.

Wrong source skills or random pairings can harm target performance.

Pairing frames by action chunks: “only to form these pairs, not as behavior-cloning targets.” Source ↗

Workshop paper · Scaling H2R: Scaling Laws and Diversity in Human-to-Robot Workshop

Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs

Junhyeong Park, Wook Jung, Taeyoung Kim, Huiwon Jang, Jinwoo Shin

Primary paper reviewed

This Scaling H2R workshop contribution adapts a robot-pretrained VLA with unpaired human and robot demonstrations. It tackles two interfaces separately. A hand-geometry training objective aligns the policy’s observation representation, while a shared action tokenizer uses independent human and robot reconstruction decoders instead of forcing both sources through one mapping. Human actions are reconstructed and retargeted to a canonical wrist–hand convention before tokenization. The tokenizer is frozen during policy adaptation, and the reported transfer uses a fixed human-trained decoder branch whose outputs already follow that control convention. Real-robot experiments cover object transfer and skills introduced through human demonstrations in a shared environment. The reported task scores include partial progress, so they must not be presented as binary success percentages. Each comparison condition uses one independently trained policy; the evidence is narrower than unrestricted cross-embodiment or in-the-wild generalization.

Research details
How it worksAlign visual features through hand geometry and share action latents while keeping separate human and robot decoders.
Why it mattersObservation alignment and action decoding are different problems; sharing a latent space need not require one identical decoder.
Open questionDoes the bridge generalize across different environments, robot embodiments, and repeated training runs beyond the tested object and skill families?
Reviewed primary source ↗Organizer listing ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed primary manuscript abstract and detailed methodological/evaluation appendix: geometry adapter, action tokenizer/decoders, training interfaces, transfer conditions, scoring and rollout protocol. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Human and robot demonstrations are collected in the same environment in the controlled transfer study.

Scores are weighted task progress, not binary success rates.

Each reported condition uses one independently trained policy; target-task rollout groups are limited.

Human-only adaptation still starts from a robot-pretrained backbone.

The default human decoder emits already-retargeted canonical actions; this does not demonstrate direct deployment of raw human anatomy.

Embodiment-specific reconstruction decoders: “independent temporal blocks and output heads” Source ↗

Task-progress scoring: “weighted task score to capture partial execution” Source ↗

Workshop paper · The Science of Physical AI Safety Workshop (SPAIS)

A Unified Bellman Operator for Safety-Critical Physical AI systems

Workshop listing indexed

Short excerpt from the listed abstract

Robot learning in safety-critical domains requires maximizing task performance while strictly adhering to safety constraints. Existing safe learning paradigms *typically* force a trade-off: they either require *a priori* knowledge to provide strict safety guarantees (e.g., safety filters), or they enable joint learning but only satisfy safety constraints on average. In this work, we propose a novel Bellman operator that unifies performance and safety objectives into a single *joint* value function…

Short excerpt from the listed abstract

Just as humans form an intention before committing muscles to movement, vision-language-action (VLA) models must bridge high-level semantic reasoning with low-level physical control, yet this translation remains opaque. Token-based steering methods, carried over from language-model interpretability, presume that semantic representations naming motion concepts execute them. Workshop paper · Workshop on Agentic Robotics

EMBODIEDSWE: Coding Agents for Long Horizon Dexterous Robotics

Yilang Liu, Zeyu Shen, Haoxiang You, Zhicheng Zheng, Lihan Zha, Kashu Yamazaki, Mingtong Zhang, Suning Huang, Jiankai Sun, Qianzhong Chen, Luxi He, Kaiyuan Liu, Haoran Chang, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Mac Schwager, Dhruv Shah, Peter Henderson, Ian Abraham, Canwen Xu

Primary paper reviewed

EmbodiedSWE separates coding agents as task solvers from coding agents as sources of policy supervision. Its benchmark contains human-designed long-horizon, contact-rich simulation tasks. Agents inspect privileged simulator state and iteratively produce executable solution programs; an isolated grader checks submitted artifacts. Verified solutions then seed EmbodiedSWE-Gen, which diversifies scenes, strategies, intermediate phases and perturbations, retaining trajectories after grader and replay checks. Those demonstrations fine-tune VLAs, so the resulting neural policy update is distinct from the coding agent’s program search. The authors test data scaling and held-out variations, and show a real four-stage lamp-disassembly example trained only on generated simulation demonstrations. That physical result covers one task and ten trials, with limited full-task completion. Appendix I also distinguishes these component studies from a broader synthetic-task-generation-to-policy pipeline that has not been run end to end. A separate exploratory RL post-training experiment for the coding agent lacks held-out checkpoint evaluation. The work provides a useful teacher-data route, not proof that all coding-agent capability has already been distilled into a general robot.

Research details
How it worksCoding agents solve simulated tasks; verified solutions are diversified into demonstrations that fine-tune VLAs, with separate program-search and learned-policy evaluations.
Why it mattersExplains a concrete route from executable solutions to policy-training data without equating program search with neural learning.
Open questionHow much capability transfers through a fully automatic generation-to-policy pipeline, and does it generalize beyond the limited real-robot study?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary arXiv v2 benchmark design, solver protocol, task/embodiment transfer, supporting-tool study, demonstration-generation methods, VLA training/generalization experiments, real-robot transfer and Appendix I limitations were read. Complete appendix implementation/prompt/result listings were not reviewed exhaustively. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Coding-agent solver experiments use full simulator state, engineered control interfaces and human-designed tasks; their success is not a direct test of vision-only deployment autonomy.

The physical VLA transfer study covers one four-stage lamp task over ten trials, with 20% cumulative full completion; it should not become a general claim of reliable long-horizon real-robot control.

Appendix I says the broader synthetic-task construction, solution generation, diversification and policy-learning pipeline has not been studied end to end.

Exploratory RL post-training of the coding agent lacks held-out checkpoint evaluation, and broader dexterous-hand embodiments remain open questions.

§3 Evaluating Coding Agents as Solvers / L120–122: “optimizing a program rather than the parameters of a learned policy.” Source ↗

§4.1 Data Engine / L287: “Generated trajectories are retained only if they pass the task grader and an open-loop replay check.” Source ↗

Appendix I / L2036–2042: “we have not yet run this pipeline end to end” Source ↗

Workshop paper · Workshop on Agentic Robotics

PhysCaP: Grounding Code-as-Policy Agent with Physics-Informed Exploration

Chen-Yu Lin, Jing-Wen Chen, Hsueh-En Chang, Hung-An Chen, Sheng-Hsun Chang, Chi-Pin Huang, Fu-En Yang, Min-Hung Chen, Yi-Ting Chen, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Shao-Hua Sun

Primary paper reviewed

PhysCaP gives a code-as-policy agent explicit ways to acquire physical information that an image alone may not reveal. Training-free modules estimate object mass using differential joint torque during a lift and stiffness using gripper force-displacement measurements. A Planner decides what information is missing and when exploration can stop; a Prioritizer filters and orders candidate interactions; a coding agent produces programs that call measurement and control APIs. Measurements update a task belief before further exploration or execution. The evaluated improvement is therefore in information gathering and programmatic control, rather than a new neural policy trained online. The study reports three physical tabletop tasks and a simulated hidden-mass task, with component comparisons that distinguish having measurement tools from choosing efficient interactions. Interaction-count and execution-time statistics are conditional on successful episodes. Simulation exposes a mass-sensing API only after a verified lift. These conditions are important when interpreting comparisons with passive policies; the experiments do not establish that all VLAs lack active perception or that the agent can infer arbitrary physics.

Research details
How it worksA Planner and Prioritizer choose informative interactions; code calls training-free mass and stiffness measurement APIs, updates task beliefs, and executes a grounded plan.
Why it mattersShows improved decisions through physical measurements and program changes, rather than neural policy retraining.
Open questionAre measurements and exploration choices reliable on new hardware and materials, including failed episodes omitted from efficiency statistics?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary arXiv v2 main text through methods, real/simulation experiments, discussion and conclusion/limitations was read; primary project page and workshop publication note were also read. ARK returned a mismatched HPC-paper body under this title, which was rejected and not used. Appendices were not reviewed comprehensively. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The implementation estimates a narrow set of physical quantities with particular robot/gripper measurements; it is not a general physical-property inference system.

Object interactions and execution time are reported only for successful episodes. Lower interaction counts alone do not establish better overall success or cost.

The simulated sensing API reveals ground-truth mass after a required lift; conclusions about VLA comparisons should remain scoped to that observation/API contract and the tested checkpoints.

The authors identify VLM variability, localization/depth precision and robot communication/execution latency as practical limitations. The mismatched indexed body was discarded.

Workshop paper · Workshop on Agentic Robotics

ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics

Runyu Lu, Yubo Wu, Ethan Kou, Haotian Lin, Letian Fu, Wenli Xiao, Ajay Mandlekar, Yinzhen Xu, Guanya Shi, Ken Goldberg, Ang Chen, Mosharaf Chowdhury, Jan Kautz, Yuke Zhu, Linxi Fan, Guanzhi Wang

Primary paper reviewed

ASPIRE learns robot control programs and reusable repair knowledge while keeping its underlying LLM frozen. Its execution engine exposes per-primitive multimodal traces so an actor can locate failures in perception, planning, grasping or control. Evolutionary search explores several candidate programs using debug seeds. Validated repairs are proposed as compact skill guidance containing a failure signature, when-to-apply condition, repair strategy and sometimes a code sketch. A fresh verifier actor checks a proposed skill on its source task before admission, and later actors retrieve the library as context. The learned artifact is thus executable code and persistent repair guidance, not an online update to the LLM’s neural weights. Evaluation separates debug and held-out seeds, with distinct procedures for different benchmarks. Simulation-discovered skills help real-robot debugging, but the paper explicitly says transfer is not direct policy deployment. The real cube study still uses human task guidance, scrambling and scene resets. One-time skill admission also leaves stale or misleading entries as an unresolved scaling issue.

Research details
How it worksA coding agent uses primitive-level traces to repair robot programs; candidate search and a verifier admit reusable repair guidance into a persistent skill library.
Why it mattersMakes the learned artifact explicit: programs and in-context repair skills, with a frozen LLM and bounded evaluation.
Open questionHow should skills be revalidated as tasks or APIs change, and what human reset and calibration support remains necessary?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary arXiv v2 introduction, execution-engine/skill-library/evolutionary-search methods, curriculum and backward transfer, main evaluation protocol, zero-shot/real-robot studies, ablations and stated limitations were read. Detailed appendix prompts and all per-task results were not reviewed exhaustively. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The underlying LLM is frozen, and its strength plus the predefined perception/planning/control API bounds expressible behavior.

Real-robot skill transfer is guidance for further physical debugging, not a policy copied directly from simulation. Human task guidance, cube scrambling and scene resets remain in the cube experiment.

Skills are checked once at admission and not revalidated as the library grows, so entries can become stale, redundant or misleading.

Reported cube efficiency is amortized time/token cost per completed turn across three episodes; total episode duration is not monotonically decreasing.

Workshop paper · Workshop on Agentic Robotics

RLE-Bench: A Qualifying Exam for Coding Agents as Robot Learning Engineers

Haitong Ma, Chenxiao Gao, Rushi Qiang, Bo Dai, Na Li

Primary project reviewed

RLE-Bench evaluates a coding agent’s robot-learning engineering process, not only the controller it finally produces. Nine tasks span interactive control, policy development, perception and estimation, and mechanical design. Depending on the task, the submitted artifact may be retained agent context, a harness for a fresh agent, an exported policy, a training recipe, an estimator or a mechanical design. The benchmark constrains development time, interactions and compute, then tests the result under hidden conditions. Its overview also distinguishes three interface levels: low-level APIs, reusable robotics tools, and privileged simulator state. These interfaces matter when interpreting agent comparisons. The public technical report includes cases in which visible objectives or development tests fail to predict broader checks, reinforcing the value of independently held-out evaluation. The benchmark does not establish field reliability for generalist robots: some transfer is explicitly sim-to-sim, aggregate charts were unreadable here, and reported API cost excludes simulation and GPU infrastructure.

Research details
How it worksGive coding agents bounded development tasks; independently evaluate their harnesses, policies, recipes or designs under hidden conditions across four workflow families.
Why it mattersMeasures engineering artifacts under hidden tests; benchmark scores and API costs do not establish field reliability or total deployment cost.
Open questionWhich engineering improvements persist on real hardware, new tasks and distributions when cost also includes infrastructure?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Complete primary project overview and technical blog read, including nine task definitions, development budgets, hidden-evaluation protocols and case studies. The arXiv manuscript was not indexed, and the PDF reader did not return it. Dynamic aggregate score charts were not readable and are not treated as verified numeric results. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The benchmark measures bounded engineering tasks; it does not establish commercial generalist deployment reliability.

The motion-tracking transfer described in the report is MuJoCo-Warp to MuJoCo-C, explicitly sim-to-sim.

API cost excludes simulation, GPU compute and other infrastructure.

Dynamic aggregate results were unavailable to this reader, so no complete current leaderboard ranking or numerical model comparison is claimed.

Published case studies are selected examples, not measured failure frequencies.

Workshop paper · Workshop on Agentic Robotics

Can Astra Solve RoboMME without Breaking the Bank?

Bingao Chen, Haoquan Fang, Karen Liu

Primary paper reviewed

Astra/RoboMME separates subtask reasoning, progress monitoring and action execution. A LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct monitor, called System 1.5 by the authors, checks each action chunk while π0.5 retains the current subtask instruction. Completion or task-specific events can trigger another Astra decision. The monitor is a particular implementation with learned supervision and task configuration, rather than a standard layer required by every robot. The simulator pauses while Astra reasons, and the paper does not provide matched monitor-versus-always-replan ablations, monetary or token-cost measurements, or a full account of monitor errors in a continuously running loop.

Research details
How it worksUse an adapted vision-language monitor to check action chunks and trigger higher-level subtask reasoning on completion or configured events.
Why it mattersMakes the monitoring interface between slower reasoning and an action policy explicit.
Open questionHow well do the monitor and replanning rules work when physical dynamics continue during reasoning?
Reviewed primary source ↗Paper record ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary manuscript introduction, methods in Sections 2.3–2.4 and evaluation limitations in Section 4 reviewed. No independent reproduction or accepted-version confirmation.

Task-specific history, prompt templates and event rules remain part of the setup.

The simulator pauses during higher-level planning.

Matched ablations, monetary/token-cost measurements and monitor-error evaluation remain incomplete.

Additional research · 2022 · Foundational paper

Code as Policies: Language Model Programs for Embodied Control

Primary paper reviewed

Code-writing language models translate instructions into executable robot programs that process perception outputs and call control APIs. This is a concrete example of writing the policy representation directly, rather than updating a neural policy through reinforcement learning.

Research details
How it worksFew-shot examples → hierarchical Python generation → perception and control APIs → reactive loops or waypoint actions. Undefined helper functions can be generated recursively.
Open primary source ↗
Read alongside these talks
Hang Zhao — Organizing Physical AI Across TimescalesJim Fan — GR00T 2 and Agentic RoboticsGoogle DeepMind / Gemini Robotics 2.5
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary manuscript text was read through the supported indexed-paper reader. Claims and limitations are paraphrases; benchmark figures are not treated as independently reproduced results.

The policy remains limited by available perception APIs and control primitives.

Cross-embodiment API adaptation is described as brittle; complex instructions outside the prompt examples can fail.

The method assumes feasible instructions and cannot establish the correctness of generated code before execution.

Discussion and Limitations: “Our approach also assumes all given instructions are feasible, and we cannot tell if a response will be correct a priori.” Source ↗

Fast-WAM keeps video co-training but skips explicit future-video generation at inference, extracting a latent world representation for actions. Compare it with DreamZero’s joint video/action policy and with explicit cloth-planning rollouts.

Additional research · 2026 · Conference project

GR00T 2: Scaling Robot Foundation Models for Generalization, Dexterity, and Adaptation

Primary project reviewed

GR00T 2 is a world-action model that jointly predicts future video and robot actions. Its official material separates three improvement mechanisms: policy post-training and real-world RL, an execution agent invoking the WAM API, and ASPIRE-authored code recovery skills. The agent watches for stalls, calls a code skill to repair the scene, then hands control back. Turbo compresses the video representation and model for onboard execution, with SONIC providing faster whole-body control.

Primary project methods and evaluation text read on 2026-11-22; performance claims remain author-reported.

The project page reports its own tasks and protocols. Target tasks absent from target-robot data may still occur in human or other-robot data. The page also reports limits of visual steering: marks do not encode final object orientation or all motion, and some long tasks still rarely complete.

Additional research · 2026 · Conference project

GRAIL: Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models

Primary project reviewed

GRAIL grounds video generation in known 3D assets before reconstruction: geometry, cameras, metric scale and a robot-proportioned character are fixed inputs. Recovered human-object interaction is retargeted to a humanoid, then object-aware and scene-aware trackers convert it into robot-action data for downstream visual policy learning. This is a generated-training-data pipeline, rather than the robot performing online search in a video model.

Additional research · 2026 · Conference project

RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies

Primary project reviewed

RoboTTT integrates test-time-training layers into a robot policy. Their fast weights are fixed-size recurrent state: incoming tokens update those weights, and the updated state conditions actions. Sequence action forcing and truncated backpropagation enable long-sequence training. DAgger Distillation uses mistakes as context and corrections as action targets, giving a mechanism for within-episode recovery.

Open primary source ↗
Read alongside these talks
RoboTTT
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary project methods and evaluation text read on 2026-11-22; performance claims remain author-reported.

Fast weights and persistent trained parameters play different roles. The reviewed assembly evaluations demonstrate context-dependent behavior; they do not establish that slow policy weights continually update across real deployments.

Additional research · 2026 · Conference project

SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model

Primary project reviewed

SuperMimic learns one differentiable world model of shared humanoid dynamics and jointly trains a tracking policy through imagined short rollouts. Gradients pass through the learned model rather than the rigid-body simulator. Its main contribution is amortizing this learning across a motion library, giving a practical alternative to repeatedly training specialists or using cluster-scale model-free RL.

FlowEval: How Much Adaptation Does an Embodied Foundation Model Need at Deployment?

Primary paper reviewed

FlowEval uses a small set of successful target-domain demonstrations and the flow-matching objective to diagnose model–deployment fit without training. It probes predictive agreement and studies whether the score correlates with improvement as adaptation data is added. It supplies a useful decision layer before collecting another large dataset: diagnose what adaptation may remain, then test that prediction.

VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning

VLRLA conditions actions on accumulated observations, actions, rewards and termination signals while keeping deployed model parameters fixed. Its in-context RL module learns during training how to use interaction history; deployment then changes the history rather than optimizing the checkpoint. The paper includes simulation studies and real tasks with cross-episode reward memory.

Additional research · 2026 · Related paper

Dual-Stream Memory for Vision-Language-Action Policies

Primary paper reviewed

Dual-Stream Memory separates compressed execution-stage context from selective access to historical visual detail. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet produces a compact temporal token; a task-conditioned retriever keeps relevant frames with spatial detail. This refines the memory question from “how long a context?” to “which information should be compressed, and which must remain accessible?”.

The authors call for matched full-system ablations and broader task/hardware tests, especially identity tracking through cup swaps.

ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions

Primary paper reviewed

ODE Policy learns a vector field for how robot commands evolve in physical time, then integrates it to produce an action trajectory. This is different from the denoising time of a generative flow head. The paper studies seamless chunk joins, small perturbations near demonstrations and a diversity head, with comparisons in imitation learning, VLA/WAM action heads and humanoid reinforcement learning.

Early Warning Signals for OpenVLA Failure under Visual Distribution Shift

Small monitors trained on internal OpenVLA activations can detect approaching failure under controlled visual occlusion. The useful distinction is between a predictive warning signal and a recovery action that actually makes the robot safer.

Primary manuscript text was read through the supported indexed-paper reader. Claims and limitations are paraphrases; benchmark figures are not treated as independently reproduced results.

The experimental setup uses five LIBERO-10 task IDs with a limited rollout budget.

Neighboring rollout states are correlated; the authors explicitly treat their result as controlled-setting decodability and call for episode-grouped and task-held-out evaluation.

A warning score alone is not a recovery policy; no-op, abort and held-action interventions are diagnostics.

SID separates bringing the robot back into familiar approach states from performing the local manipulation. An object-centric motion field aligns the scene to a demonstrated support region, then an egocentric flow-matching policy executes the skill.

ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World

Primary project reviewed

ENPIRE makes selected physical manipulation tasks accessible to coding agents as repeatable research environments. Its Environment component resets scenes and verifies outcomes; Policy Improvement launches a chosen refinement routine; Rollout evaluates candidates on one or more robots; Evolution lets coding agents inspect failures and modify algorithm or infrastructure code. The improvement interface accepts several regimes, including heuristics, code/tool use, behavior cloning, offline RL and online RL. Consequently, the changed artifact can be an executable program, a training recipe or a learned policy, depending on the experiment. The project describes agent-run iterations on prepared tasks such as Push-T and pin insertion, together with simulation experiments and fleet-resource measurements. This is evidence of an engineered loop around real interaction, rather than merely a supervisor choosing skills during one episode. Its autonomy claim is scoped to the provided self-resetting, self-verifying task interfaces. The site labels its showcased 99% result as pass@8, so it should not be rewritten as single-attempt reliability. All results remain author-reported.

HARBOR: A Harness Framework for Agentic Robot Reinforcement Learning

Primary paper reviewed

HARBOR automates the engineering workflow surrounding robot reinforcement learning in simulation. A central agent divides a request into bounded stages such as dependencies, task construction, rewards, domain randomization, RL integration and tuning. Stage-local agents operate through standard commands and persistent artifacts. Executable gates check interfaces and rollout evidence before later stages proceed; failures are repaired within a retry budget and unresolved stages can require human intervention. Reward and hyperparameter candidates run in isolated parallel trials, while an experience ledger preserves useful heuristics and failure diagnoses for later runs. This separates the coding agent that constructs or tunes the experiment from the numerical RL algorithm that trains the policy. The authors evaluate multiple simulation backends and include physical validation, but the latter uses user-provided real trajectories, interface engineering and human feedback for simulator alignment. The source explicitly warns that gates do not guarantee semantic policy correctness. Its results support a scoped engineering-automation claim, not a general guarantee that any agent can autonomously train reliable real-world policies.

Research details
How it worksStage-specific agents build simulation tasks, rewards and training configurations; executable gates check artifacts, parallel RL trials compare candidates, and experience ledgers preserve useful engineering lessons.
Why it mattersSeparates the agent’s engineering decisions from RL’s parameter updates and makes intermediate evidence inspectable.
Open questionHow much prior scaffolding and human engineering remains necessary for unfamiliar tasks and real-robot transfer?

MobiAgent: Dual-Loop Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation

Primary paper reviewed

MobiAgent separates deployment-time planning from offline policy refinement. Its inner loop uses a VLM planner, a shared VLM trunk with skill-specific flow-matching action experts, and a reflection critic that recommends advance, retry or replan. Critic observations are retained as episode memory. The outer loop runs after episode termination: it segments and verifies trajectories, standardizes skill captions and trains or fine-tunes neural skill policies. Startup data creates the skill inventory; subsequent rollout data is assigned to the existing inventory, and the described continual phase updates those existing policies without expanding the model inventory. This is more specific than saying the robot simply learns through reasoning or that its skill vocabulary grows without bound. The authors report finite deployment-to-training rounds on RoboCasa and Astribot S1, plus long-horizon BEHAVIOR tasks. Early RoboCasa gains later plateau. Here the reusable changes are learned skill policies and curated data; the paper does not establish indefinite improvement or a learning procedure that recursively redesigns itself.

Research details
How it worksAn online planner and critic compose learned skills; after episodes, verified rollout clips fine-tune the existing skill policies offline.
Why it mattersDistinguishes execution-time memory from later parameter learning using deployment data.

PhysCaP: Grounding Code-as-Policy Agent with Physics-Informed Exploration

Primary paper reviewed

PhysCaP gives a code-as-policy agent explicit ways to acquire physical information that an image alone may not reveal. Training-free modules estimate object mass using differential joint torque during a lift and stiffness using gripper force-displacement measurements. A Planner decides what information is missing and when exploration can stop; a Prioritizer filters and orders candidate interactions; a coding agent produces programs that call measurement and control APIs. Measurements update a task belief before further exploration or execution. The evaluated improvement is therefore in information gathering and programmatic control, rather than a new neural policy trained online. The study reports three physical tabletop tasks and a simulated hidden-mass task, with component comparisons that distinguish having measurement tools from choosing efficient interactions. Interaction-count and execution-time statistics are conditional on successful episodes. Simulation exposes a mass-sensing API only after a verified lift. These conditions are important when interpreting comparisons with passive policies; the experiments do not establish that all VLAs lack active perception or that the agent can infer arbitrary physics.

ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics

Primary paper reviewed

ASPIRE learns robot control programs and reusable repair knowledge while keeping its underlying LLM frozen. Its execution engine exposes per-primitive multimodal traces so an actor can locate failures in perception, planning, grasping or control. Evolutionary search explores several candidate programs using debug seeds. Validated repairs are proposed as compact skill guidance containing a failure signature, when-to-apply condition, repair strategy and sometimes a code sketch. EmbodiedSWE: Coding Agents for Long Horizon Dexterous Robotics

Primary paper reviewed

EmbodiedSWE separates coding agents as task solvers from coding agents as sources of policy supervision. Its benchmark contains human-designed long-horizon, contact-rich simulation tasks. Agents inspect privileged simulator state and iteratively produce executable solution programs; an isolated grader checks submitted artifacts. Verified solutions then seed EmbodiedSWE-Gen, which diversifies scenes, strategies, intermediate phases and perturbations, retaining trajectories after grader and replay checks. Those demonstrations fine-tune VLAs, so the resulting neural policy update is distinct from the coding agent’s program search. The authors test data scaling and held-out variations, and show a real four-stage lamp-disassembly example trained only on generated simulation demonstrations. That physical result covers one task and ten trials, with limited full-task completion. Appendix I also distinguishes these component studies from a broader synthetic-task-generation-to-policy pipeline that has not been run end to end. A separate exploratory RL post-training experiment for the coding agent lacks held-out checkpoint evaluation. The work provides a useful teacher-data route, not proof that all coding-agent capability has already been distilled into a general robot.

This study asks how a fixed demonstration budget should be distributed across instruction factors, rather than treating data scale as a single count. H2RBench compares human-to-robot transfer methods under a shared task and supervision protocol. Imitation from Heterogeneous Demonstrations using Grounded Latent-Action World Models

Primary paper reviewed

GLAM learns a shared latent-action representation from target robot demonstrations and cheaper auxiliary trajectories that need not carry executable action labels. One model infers latent actions from visual transitions; another uses target action labels to make those latents decodable into robot control. An asymmetric alignment loss transfers the target branch’s control information into the transition-based representation. The resulting model relabels heterogeneous trajectories for a downstream imitation policy. The authors test Kinova robot data and a simulated floating-UMI-gripper source, with an object-mask variant to emphasize manipulated-object motion. They report data-efficiency gains and useful auxiliary-data scaling in these settings. This is evidence for control-grounded representation as an alternative to simply sharing raw action coordinates. It is not demonstrated web-video or human-hand transfer: the source and target share scenes, camera placement, objects and task semantics, and tactile or force information is absent.

Additional research · 2026 · Workshop contribution

RARA: Robust Policy Fine-Tuning through Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment for Robotic Manipulation

Primary paper reviewed

RARA reuses selected pretraining demonstrations to guide task adaptation. It retrieves trajectories by instruction similarity, then matches target frames to relevant source phases by action-chunk similarity. First it trains representation-producing layers and a small projector to align target features with frozen pretrained features. It then behavior-clones the target task while constraining how the policy represents the retrieved source observations. Retrieved source actions form alignment pairs; they are not extra behavior-cloning targets. In the reported diffusion-policy and GR00T experiments, this combination improves adaptation under visual shifts. Data choice is crucial: using unrelated pretraining skills or random pairings can remove the gain and sometimes hurt performance. The method therefore supplies a selection-and-preservation perspective on post-training, rather than a claim that anchoring any prior representation is beneficial. The experiments keep the robot and action space fixed and require relevant pretraining data.

Research details
How it worksRetrieve relevant pretraining trajectories, align target features to their pretrained features, then fine-tune while anchoring source representations.
Why it mattersUseful prior data can preserve representations; unrelated reference skills can instead harm adaptation.
Open questionHow can suitable anchors be found without related pretraining data, or when embodiment and action space change?

Memory Anchors studies which old experiences help a robot policy retain earlier tasks during sequential learning. It identifies new-task observations that overlap old-task representations but require different actions, then selects nearby old experiences for replay. For diffusion policies, the project measures action disagreement through conditional denoising to reduce confusion from multiple valid action modes. Controlled experiments remove or enrich these anchors while keeping the replay budget comparable, and the authors report changes in forgetting in simulation and diagnostic real-robot task sequences. The project also emphasizes that replay cannot consist only of high-conflict anchors: diverse old experience remains important. This is persistent policy training from selected past data, not inference-time conversational memory. Extracting anchors needs the model’s representation space and past training data; the evaluated task sequences and robots do not establish unlimited continual deployment.

Research details
How it worksIdentify overlapping old/new states with conflicting actions, select nearby old experiences, and mix these anchors with diverse replay during training.
Why it mattersReplay composition can matter beyond buffer size; important old decision states help protect previous skills.
Open questionCan anchor selection work with inaccessible pretraining data, very large histories, and longer task sequences without losing replay diversity?

Additional research ·

FAR: Failure-Aware Retry for Test-Time Recovery and Continual Policy Improvement

Primary paper reviewed

FAR addresses the case in which an existing diffusion policy fails and a naive retry repeats the same behavior. It uses critic estimates to select potentially failure-inducing action chunks, pairs them with higher-valued alternatives, and performs a short preference-based policy update before retrying. Smoothed action perturbations provide local exploration. A separate improvement loop combines expert data, successful online trajectories and failed trajectories: the critic learns from the collected experience, while the actor learns from expert and successful data. The reported evaluation covers nine simulated manipulation tasks and three real xArm tasks, with bounded retry budgets. The paper supports distinguishing immediate recovery from longer-term policy improvement, but its autonomy claim needs care: real experiments use a human’s binary success/failure signal, and the arm is returned to its initial configuration between retries while the scene remains changed. Tests use single-task diffusion policies trained from scratch; transfer to large pretrained VLAs and principled automatic failure detection are stated future work.

Research details
How it worksUse critic estimates to select failure chunks, update the diffusion policy from failure/alternative preferences, and retry with smoothed perturbations. Replay recovery experience for further training.
Why it mattersSeparates immediate retry adaptation from later learning, while exposing human outcome signals and partial resets as part of the tested workflow.
Open questionDo recovery gains survive automatic failure detection, safety-constrained exploration and transfer to large pretrained policies?
Open primary source ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary manuscript main text, method (§4), experiments (§5), limitations (§6), and evaluation protocol (§C.3) read through the supported PDF-text reader; primary project page also read. Other appendix sections were not comprehensively reviewed. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The real-world protocol depends on a human-provided binary outcome signal; FAR does not supply a principled autonomous failure detector.

Retries still return the arm to an initial configuration. Avoiding full scene resets is different from eliminating every intervention.

The evaluated policies are trained from scratch in single-task settings; no demonstrated universal transfer to generalist VLAs.

Recovery exploration safety remains future work, and reported success is measured under finite retry budgets.

Appendix C.3 Evaluation, lines 1238–1241: “In real-world experiments, a human observer provides a binary success/failure signal after each attempt.” Source ↗

§6 Limitations and Future Work, lines 528–532: “our current framework does not include a principled failure detection mechanism, and instead relies on environment feedback and time limits.” Source ↗

Additional research ·

ATOM-Bench: A Real-World Benchmark for Atomic Skills and Compositional Generalization in Manipulation Policies

Primary project reviewed

ATOM-Bench separates learning elementary manipulation skills from recombining them under new task structures. Its motor set isolates physical operations, its instruction set isolates language constraints, and a held-out composition set combines those factors. Models are adapted on atomic tasks only, rather than being shown demonstrations of the compositional test tasks. The project describes paired single-arm Franka Panda and dual-arm Cobot Magic tracks, with fixed physical test seeds and metrics for task completion, partial progress and composition failures. The reported models often perform much better on atomic tasks than on held-out combinations. This is useful evidence for asking what a benchmark score actually measures: a successful familiar operation is not automatically evidence of compositional reuse. The scope remains tabletop manipulation on these platforms and these adaptation protocols, not general home or factory performance. The project page reports results for its selected policies; it does not establish that every VLA has the same failure profile.

Research details
How it worksFine-tune on atomic motor and instruction tasks, then test held-out compositions on two robot platforms using fixed physical seeds.
Why it mattersSeparates familiar skill execution from recombining skills; results remain scoped to the benchmark’s tasks, platforms and adaptation recipe.
Open questionHow stable are compositional results under more seeds, different adaptation budgets and tasks beyond tabletop manipulation?
Open primary source ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Complete primary project page read, including task factorization, real-robot platforms, adaptation/test protocol and static results. The indexed-paper reader did not contain this ID; the full manuscript was not read. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

Results are conditioned on the particular atomic-to-compositional split and the two hardware tracks.

Ten fixed physical seeds improve reproducibility but do not represent the full deployment distribution.

The displayed model comparisons concern the listed versions and training recipe; they cannot be generalized to all newer policies.

The complete primary project page was reviewed, not the full manuscript or an independent replication.

Evaluation Protocol, lines 86–100: “Models are jointly fine-tuned on all 15 atomic tasks per platform, with no composition demos.” Source ↗

Results heading, line 110: “Strong atomic performance does not guarantee held-out composition.” Source ↗

Additional research ·

ContactGuard: Pre-Contact Execution Monitoring with Action-Conditioned Latent World Models

Primary paper reviewed

ContactGuard is an execution monitor for a policy that proposes action chunks. It learns action-conditioned visual dynamics from unlabeled robot trajectories, freezes that latent world model, and trains a small failure probe on labeled pre-contact clips. Before a predicted gripper closure, the monitor rolls the model forward under the policy’s own planned actions and scores the future latent. A task-calibrated threshold can veto the chunk while the underlying policy remains unchanged. The experiments use four grasp settings on a dual-arm robot and compare future-latent monitoring against matched current-state and action-corruption controls. The live evaluation is a controlled counterfactual protocol: flagged attempts pause before contact and then resume so the would-be outcome can be recorded. Its claim is predictive abstention, not completed autonomous recovery or policy learning. The paper explicitly leaves post-abort completion and longer-horizon monitoring for future work. It therefore supports reporting false aborts, missed failures and subsequent task completion separately.

Research details
How it worksRoll a frozen latent world model forward under the proposed action chunk; a trained failure probe can veto imminent contact.
Why it mattersPre-contact detection is separate from recovery: the published monitor abstains but does not finish the task after an abort.
Open questionCan calibration hold on new contacts while a recovery module completes vetoed tasks at an acceptable false-abort rate?
Open primary source ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Indexed primary manuscript introduction, latent-model/probe methods, online monitor, experimental setup/results and limitations read. Figures and the complete original PDF were not independently inspected. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

It abstains but does not repair the scene or complete the task after an abort.

The implemented trigger is an imminent commanded gripper closure; general contact-event triggering is not demonstrated.

Evaluation covers four grasp settings and per-task validation thresholds, not arbitrary long-horizon skills.

The live protocol pauses and resumes flagged chunks to label counterfactual outcomes; it is not an evaluation of a complete abort-and-recover system.

Conclusions, Limitations, and Future Work: “ContactGuard prevents failures by abstaining, but does not recover from them or complete the task after an abort.” Source ↗

Introduction: pre-contact monitoring: “the monitor asks whether the action it is about to execute is likely to fail.” Source ↗

Additional research ·

Multisensory Continual Learning: Adapting Pretrained Visuomotor Policies to Force

Primary paper reviewed

MuSe asks how a policy pretrained without a sensor can acquire that modality later while preserving its earlier capabilities. The studied case adds force-torque sensing to a pretrained Unified Video-Action model. Early token fusion and later cross-attention adapters combine the sensor with vision and other inputs; the model predicts future observations, force-torque signals and actions. During adaptation, replay mixes the original pretraining data with new multisensory demonstrations, masking the force input and force loss where those measurements are absent. The evaluation separates force prediction on previously unsupervised tasks, forward transfer to new contact-rich tasks and backward transfer to pretraining tasks. The authors report improvements in their tabletop settings, while no-replay ablations exhibit substantial forgetting. This is evidence for a particular sensor-expansion and replay strategy, not a result that every added sensor improves every policy. Only force-torque expansion, limited tasks and access to the original pretraining data were tested; broader modalities, embodiments and longer horizons remain future work.

Research details
How it worksAdd force-torque fusion and future prediction to pretrained UVA; mix new multisensory demonstrations with original-data replay, masking absent force inputs and losses.
Why it mattersSeparates new-sensor adaptation, old-task retention and cross-modal transfer; the tested case adds force-torque sensing.
Open questionWill retention hold without stored pretraining data, or when adding touch, audio or depth instead of force-torque?
Open primary source ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Primary v4 HTML manuscript main text (§1–5), methods, force-torque case study, ablations and limitations read. References and appendices were not comprehensively reviewed. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The demonstrated sensor-expansion case is force-torque; other modalities and combinations are untested.

Replay assumes access to the original pretraining data.

The real-world evaluation is a limited tabletop task set; diverse robots and longer-horizon tasks remain future work.

Some reported task scores use partial credit, so fractional totals should not be described as counts of independently successful trials.

§5 Limitations and future works, lines 307–311: “We study multi-sensory continual learning through a single sensor-expansion case: adding force–torque sensing to a pretrained vision-action policy.” Source ↗

Additional research ·

RLE-Bench: A Qualifying Exam for Coding Agents as Robot Learning Engineers

Primary project reviewed

RLE-Bench evaluates a coding agent’s robot-learning engineering process, not only the controller it finally produces. Nine tasks span interactive control, policy development, perception and estimation, and mechanical design. Depending on the task, the submitted artifact may be retained agent context, a harness for a fresh agent, an exported policy, a training recipe, an estimator or a mechanical design. The benchmark constrains development time, interactions and compute, then tests the result under hidden conditions. Its overview also distinguishes three interface levels: low-level APIs, reusable robotics tools, and privileged simulator state. These interfaces matter when interpreting agent comparisons. The public technical report includes cases in which visible objectives or development tests fail to predict broader checks, reinforcing the value of independently held-out evaluation. The benchmark does not establish field reliability for generalist robots: some transfer is explicitly sim-to-sim, aggregate charts were unreadable here, and reported API cost excludes simulation and GPU infrastructure.

Research details
How it worksGive coding agents bounded development tasks; independently evaluate their harnesses, policies, recipes or designs under hidden conditions across four workflow families.
Why it mattersMeasures engineering artifacts under hidden tests; benchmark scores and API costs do not establish field reliability or total deployment cost.
Open questionWhich engineering improvements persist on real hardware, new tasks and distributions when cost also includes infrastructure?
Open primary source ↗
Scope, limitations & sources

Complete primary project overview and technical blog read, including nine task definitions, development budgets, hidden-evaluation protocols and case studies. The arXiv manuscript was not indexed, and the PDF reader did not return it. Dynamic aggregate score charts were not readable and are not treated as verified numeric results. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

The benchmark measures bounded engineering tasks; it does not establish commercial generalist deployment reliability.

The motion-tracking transfer described in the report is MuJoCo-Warp to MuJoCo-C, explicitly sim-to-sim.

API cost excludes simulation, GPU compute and other infrastructure.

Dynamic aggregate results were unavailable to this reader, so no complete current leaderboard ranking or numerical model comparison is claimed.

Published case studies are selected examples, not measured failure frequencies.

Coding agents beyond the digital world, lines 18–22: “The capabilities we would like to evaluate span over the agent’s development process, not merely the policy it eventually produces.” Source ↗

Performance and Cost, lines 21–24: “Cost excludes simulation, GPU compute, and other infrastructure.” Source ↗

LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs

Primary paper reviewed

LeWAM jointly learns action-conditioned latent dynamics and a flow-matching action policy. It can sample actions directly or refine candidate plans by differentiating through the learned dynamics. Its goal-image planning experiments and goal-free behavior-cloning experiments test different uses of that model family. The physical-robot experiments use direct policy execution; they do not demonstrate that online planning improves every physical task. Models are trained or adapted for individual tasks and embodiments.

How it worksJointly train latent-state prediction and action generation; for planning, refine sampled action sequences while holding model parameters fixed.

Additional research · 2026 · Workshop research paper

Rolling-WAM: World Action Models with Rolling Imagination

Primary paper reviewed

Rolling-WAM distributes joint video-action denoising across successive control updates. It completes the next action chunk while retaining partially refined future chunks, then incorporates a new observation as the window advances. The paper evaluates simulation benchmarks and three Unitree G1 manipulation tasks. Its timing comparison measures steady-state replanning rather than startup or the complete robot lifecycle. The authors also identify a trade-off: retained future predictions can lag behind rapid scene changes, particularly with long windows.

Research details
How it worksMaintain a sliding video-action prediction window at staggered noise levels; finish, execute and replace the nearest chunk while refining its future continuation.
Why it mattersChanges how prediction compute is allocated over time, supplying another concrete timing strategy alongside the conference discussion of robot control clocks.
Open questionHow do window size and initialization cost affect response to abrupt changes outside the demonstrated task distribution?

Additional research · 2026 · Main-conference paper

ImageWAM: Do World Action Models Really Need Video Generation, or Just Image Editing?

Primary paper reviewed

ImageWAM attaches an action expert to an image-editing backbone. During inference it computes editing-aware attention context from one editing-branch step, then denoises an action chunk using that context. It does not decode a complete future image or generate a dense future video for each update. The study reports simulation benchmarks and four dual-arm hardware tasks, with multiple editing backbones. This supports examining how much visual prediction an action policy needs in those settings, rather than declaring video prediction unnecessary for all robot control.

Research details
How it worksTrain the editing branch and action expert together, retain frozen understanding components, and use editing caches to condition action flow matching.
Why it mattersSupplies a main-paper alternative to dense future-video intermediates and separates one editing-step shortcut from the remaining action-denoising computation.
Open questionWhich dynamic or longer-horizon tasks require temporal prediction that an editing-cache intermediate does not retain?

Additional research · 2026 · Main-conference paper

LaWAM: Latent World Action Models for Efficient Dynamics-Aware Robot Policies

Primary paper reviewed

LaWAM learns a latent-action-conditioned world model in a frozen visual feature space, then teaches a language-conditioned policy to predict the latent action needed for a future subgoal. An action expert uses that compact future feature without rendering future pixels. The manuscript includes physical-time alignment for mixed-frequency action data and controlled task evaluations. Its stated limitations include unstable camera motion and insufficient coverage of fine deformable dynamics. Coherent open-loop latent rollouts on other embodiments are not the same evidence as successful closed-loop control on a new robot.

Research details
How it worksPretrain latent dynamics, distill transition codes into a policy prior, and condition action chunks on a predicted latent visual subgoal.
Why it mattersConnects predictive representation design with practical action timing, while identifying where future-state features and native action frequencies enter the policy.
Open questionCan its latent dynamics retain useful task change when camera self-motion or fine contact deformation dominates the observation?

Coverage ledger

What is covered—and what is still missing.

The atlas indexes 87 supplied recording entries, a 687-paper main-conference catalogue with abstracts from an explicitly labeled secondary snapshot, and 484 published workshop entries from primary organizer pages. All 32 official workshops were checked; paper lists remain incomplete for 20 workshops, and full-manuscript and exact playback verification are tracked separately.

66 paper presentations

21 oral talks and 45 spotlights, represented by recorded source notes.

21 other recorded segments

Keynotes, industry presentations, fireside, debate and closing.

484 workshop listings

All 32 workshop pages checked. Twelve organizer lists are complete; twenty still have metadata gaps.

Research trackIndexedCurrent boundary
Main-conference oral presentations21O1–O7 contain 21 recorded oral presentations. All 21 also appear in the broader secondary catalogue. Canonical paper PDFs and official acceptance records still need direct primary verification.
Main-conference spotlight presentations45S1–S5 are indexed from supplied recordings (45 talks). The secondary catalogue includes S6–S8 metadata and all 72 spotlight abstracts. Matching the missing morning sessions to original playback remains open.
Accepted main-conference posters594The secondary main-conference snapshot includes 594 poster-only entries with titles, authors, abstracts and original OpenReview links. Acceptance counts and paper content have not yet been independently reconciled with the canonical primary portal.
Late-breaking research0Opening remarks identify agentic robotics and real-to-sim-to-real as the two themes and report 39 accepted contributions. Treat these as a separate track with distinct review and publication status.
Workshop research484All 32 workshop directory entries were checked against the official program. 484 published paper entries across 15 workshops are indexed; 12 organizer lists are complete. 51 original abstracts are available. Twenty workshops still have unresolved complete paper lists, including a published filename-only folder and selected subsets. Workshop acceptance is distinct from archival main-conference acceptance.
Keynotes, industry and discussion21Includes six keynotes, twelve industry/sponsor presentations, a fireside chat, a special debate and the closing session. Industry claims remain speaker-reported unless supported by a reviewed technical source.

Primary-source depth

The November 22 review covered twenty-one additional public sources: seventeen manuscript-section reviews and four technical project-method reviews. Three further primary-manuscript notes were added on November 25 for AMP1, RAX and the Astra/RoboMME monitor. These reviews are separate from the broader catalogue and from confirming accepted publication versions.

Recording and transcript status

Original recordings are publicly available. Transcript redistribution permission has not been established from the retrieved sources. The existing supplied transcript archive is retained; no additional bundled archive is introduced.

How evidence is treated

Recorded source reviewed means the notes were built from the supplied talk transcript. Primary paper reviewed means the paper text was retrieved and read. A reading lead has a discovered title and URL, with its contents still awaiting review.

Editorial comparisons connect mechanisms and propose useful tests; they are not attributed speaker quotations. Company claims remain speaker-reported unless supported by reviewed technical evidence. Social posts may help discover work; the cited sources are papers, project pages, technical reports and original talks.

Video starts are transcript-aligned. Automatic captions have coarse segment boundaries, so audiovisual checking is still required before claiming second-perfect timing.
